Why Does The 21,000-Pound Force On A Boeing 737 Door Keep Blended-Wing Jets Out Of Airline Service?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1670 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, since the dawn of modern commercial aviation, there have been many different planemakers and jetliners that have taken to the sky, nevertheless, there has been one constant theme that can be found in every single airframe to date.
  • According to recent reports, meanwhile, the revolutionary blended wing body concept has been championed for years as a next-generation jetliner template for its 20-30% fuel efficiency, yet it inherently conflicts with all four of these design priorities.
  • According to recent reports, pressurization systems maintain roughly 8.35 psi (0.58 bar) inside and exert about 21,000 lbs (93 kN) of force against a standard jet entry door.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, since the dawn of modern commercial aviation, there have been many different planemakers and jetliners that have taken to the sky, nevertheless, there has been one constant theme that can be found in every single airframe to date. That is the conventional tube-and-wing design, which is optimized to hold cabin pressure, scale aircraft size, simplify airport operations, and simplify evacuating passengers in an emergency.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, the revolutionary blended wing body concept has been championed for years as a next-generation jetliner template for its 20-30% fuel efficiency, yet it inherently conflicts with all four of these design priorities. One of the main design hurdles for a BWB is simply holding in the air while cruising at altitude.

According to recent reports, pressurization systems maintain roughly 8.35 psi (0.58 bar) inside and exert about 21,000 lbs (93 kN) of force against a standard jet entry door. As noted in Engineers Ireland's overview of blended-wing airliners, flattening that cabin cuts drag and could burn up, but a BWB's flat walls experience much more intense loads under that same pressure.

Industry observers note that pressurized air tries to bend flat floors and ceilings outward into a round bubble. Reinforcing the frame against that bending adds heavy internal beams and thick carbon walls, eating away fuel savings while complicating emergency exits and preventing easy fuselage stretches.

For the ZEROe hydrogen program, Airbus first displayed a 200-seat BWB in the hopes that the broad body would accommodate large fuel tanks that were chilled to -423°F (-253°C). However, in 2025, Airbus abandoned that concept for more research and went back to a traditional tube-and-wing configuration with hydrogen fuel-cell pods.

Recent findings suggest that airbus executives realized there was too much financial risk involved in certifying a pressurized passenger cabin while negotiating airport gate constraints and non-stretchable tooling, a risk that commercial airlines declined to finance. Rather, blended-wing concepts are being introduced to military forces first by aerospace developers.

Through the Defense Innovation Unit, the US Air Force awarded startup JetZero $235 million in August 2023 to construct a full-scale demonstrator using Northrop Grumman's Scaled Composites for flight testing in 2027. Designed for next-generation aerial refueling and military cargo missions, the JetZero demonstrator mounts two commercial high-bypass engines above the rear wing body.

According to recent reports, while high-angle takeoffs can push turbulent airflow into top-mounted engine fans, this layout cuts ground noise and protects engines from runway debris. More significantly, gasoline tanks and freight pallets do not require windows, never experience airsickness, and completely circumvent passenger evacuation regulations. Before going back to passenger aircraft, developers intend to reduce the financial and engineering risks.

Sources indicate that they will do so by first demonstrating composite pressure structures and flight-control software in military cargo and tanker operations. Commercial passengers will continue to board well-known round jets until military flights demonstrate that internal bracing can safely retain cabin air without significant weight penalties or emergency evacuation bottlenecks, leaving the BWB to earn its wings in uniform.

Sources indicate that over 80% of travelers inside a 250-seat BWB will sit in windowless center bays, forcing airlines to install heavy, maintenance-prone digital wall screens instead of simple windows. Additionally, passengers at the outboard edge have a rougher ride during turns because the outer seats sit 40-50 feet (12-15 meters) away from the centerline.

During a standard 30-degree banked turn or a bumpy crosswind landing, outer-row flyers do not just tilt gently. They will feel a swing through wide arcs that may trigger airsickness much more frequently. Planemakers manufacturing a BWB will have to divide the cabin with permanent structural support walls in order to contain the immense outward air pressure inside a wide BWB.

To prevent flat panels from protruding outward, these vertical composite ties secure the floor directly to the ceiling. Although this interior grid prevents blowout without adding undue weight, it divides the cabin into cubicle-like bays that make it difficult for airlines to later modify legroom or move seats. On the land side, guiding 250 or more travelers through a standard jet bridge into a wide, multi-aisle grid creates bottlenecks at the entrance.

Sources indicate that standard airport jet bridges only connect to one or two forward left-hand doors. The unique shape and depth of the belly hold will also fundamentally alter the way that baggage and cargo handling is done. Ultimately, even when the first BWB does take flight, there remain many unresolved dilemmas to be overcome before the first arrives on the flight line at an airport near you.

Industry observers note that mainline passenger jets like the Boeing 737 MAX, Airbus A321neo, and Boeing 777-300ER are iconic examples of a typical tubular-and-wing design with minimal dead weight. The optimized, thin skin of each plane's fuselage stretches uniformly like a balloon as internal pressure pushes outward equally in all directions.

Industry observers note that this design premise is upset when that barrel is flattened and morphed into the cabin of a BWB. A cylindrical hull allows even composite aircraft, like a Boeing 787 Dreamliner, to withstand decades of pressurized flight without the need for a more complex airframe. Engineering studies show that internal bending can multiply structural stress more than tenfold compared to a simple round tube.

According to recent reports, panels bow from air pushing on the concentrated points of floors and ceilings. Stopping the cabin from bursting at the seams forces makers to add bracing and load-bearing bulkheads. Building a BWB cabin strong enough to hold normal cruise pressure therefore requires exceptionally thick carbon skin and heavy framing.

Recent findings suggest that the weight of additional support then directly reduces the 20-30% fuel burn reduction claimed by BWBs, complicating manufacturing and operating trade-offs. Another problem with blended-wing aircraft is that they are nearly impossible to scale up to larger models, even if engineers can overcome the significant cabin weight issue.

On July 20, 2007, the subscale Boeing-NASA X-48B demonstrated that flight computers could control a tailless flying wing above Edwards Air Force Base. Through 2010, the 500 lbs (227-kg) test plane had 92 successful flights, thanks to three small jet engines producing 52 lbs of thrust (0.23 kN each).

Despite NASA's X-48B passing the flight tests, building a full-size airplane provides serious day-to-day flying challenges. Standard jets mount their tail fins roughly 100 feet (30 m) behind the aircraft's balance point, giving tail flaps high leverage to lift the nose during takeoff. Without a long tail, a BWB relies on large rear wing flaps to pitch the nose upward.

In a recent development, deflecting those flaps sharply during takeoff actually spills lift right when pilots need it most on the runway. Despite these hurdles, developers are actively testing practical engineering solutions. According to CNN's report on the JetZero program, the US Air Force-backed startup uses lightweight composite panels and internal ribs to tame cabin pressure without excessive weight.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, Nautilus avoids pressure penalties on its unpressurized KONA cargo plane while giving its Horizon Evo passenger jet a narrower, double-deck center body that limits bending stress and fits standard 737 airport gates. Still, an even bigger problem for airlines and aircraft makers is fleet growth.

Manufacturers build profitable aircraft families, like stretching the Airbus A320 into the A321neo or growing the Boeing 737 into the MAX 10, by simply inserting round barrel sections ahead of and behind the wings. By using the same basic wing design, pilot training, and replacement components, airlines are able to carry more passengers.

Meanwhile, they maintain fair purchase and operating costs thanks to this simple production technique. That straightforward stretch option is eliminated by a BWB, which integrates the cabin directly into the wing's curved lifting shape.

Sources indicate that the smooth airflow of the wing is ruined, and the plane's balancing point is shifted when the middle body is cut apart to accommodate additional rows. In order to create a larger version, producers would have to completely redo the flight-control software, redesign the exterior shell, and rework the internal wing beams, which would cost billions of dollars for each size of seat.

Industry observers note that one of the greatest functional hurdles for blended-wing designs is that every commercial airport on Earth is built for a traditional tube-and-wing jet. A 250-seat blended-wing plane would span nearly 200 feet (61 meters), which is on par with the Boeing 777-9 and Airbus A350-1000, bringing higher airport fees and slower turnarounds.

Sources indicate that conventional large airliners, like the 747 and A380, were already met with major resistance as their wingspans forced airports to widen taxiways and rebuild gates. As detailed in Leeham News' analysis of blended-wing airliners, wide-wingspan planes are vital for lowering drag and improving fuel burn, yet the A380 directly suffered in sales due to its limited destination portfolio.

That restriction on airport access keeps airlines cautious, as it is a hard bottleneck on network versatility and therefore business utility. To date, no carrier holds a firm, deposit-backed order for a BWB. Given that commercial carriers will not fund the certification risks upfront, developers have turned to military applications to make the BWB a reality.

When JetZero's full-scale demonstration flies for the US military in 2027, aviation leaders will be present at Edwards Air Force Base. These test flights will assess computer flight controls, aerial refueling management, and composite fabrication. Military missions may demonstrate that internal composite bracing can hold cabin air without adding excessive structural weight.

If so, commercial designers researching new passenger airliners for the late 2030s may eventually profit from that flight data. Until planemakers demonstrate that a BWB can withstand rigorous 90-second emergency evacuation testing without incurring substantial structural penalties, customers will continue to board conventional jets.

At 37,000 feet (11,278 m), the physics of maintaining breathable air remains relentlessly demanding. The basic tube will continue to dominate aviation economics because a simple metal or composite cylinder can withstand 21,000 lbs (93 kN) of outward door force with little material weight.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Travelers are conditioned to expect high prices at airport retailers and restaurants, so over $5 for a bottle of water at an airport shop, or $25 for a burger at a mediocre airport restaurant, might not catch anyone off guard.
  • It has been revealed that however, did you know there are caps on how much retailers at airports are supposed to be able to charge, and they’re largely just not enforced?
  • Industry observers note that airports generate revenue in a variety of ways, and one of the major ways is through the retailers they have in the terminal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Travelers are conditioned to expect high prices at airport retailers and restaurants, so over $5 for a bottle of water at an airport shop, or $25 for a burger at a mediocre airport restaurant, might not catch anyone off guard.

It has been revealed that however, did you know there are caps on how much retailers at airports are supposed to be able to charge, and they’re largely just not enforced? Well, or perhaps more accurately, they are enforced, but using very dishonest math. The backstory of this is interesting.

Industry observers note that airports generate revenue in a variety of ways, and one of the major ways is through the retailers they have in the terminal. An airport is like a shopping mall with a very captive audience, and as you’d expect, rent for businesses in airports is absolutely through the roof, as a result of that.

But in order to balance things out and prevent retailers from exploiting consumers, over 80% of airports in the United States specifically stipulate the maximum prices that airports can charge consumers. These terms are typically baked into the contracts that airport retailers sign, and failure to adhere to the rules can lead to consequences, at least in theory.

The airports with pricing caps for airport businesses generally fall into one of two categories:.

According to recent reports, if there are supposed to be rules in place capping airport pricing, then why is this such a widespread matter? More Perfect Union recently published a great video investigating this issue, and it’s a fascinating watch. First they actually analyze airport pricing, and then they confront airport authorities about the lack of enforcement.

According to recent reports, here’s what’s interesting — airport retailers do have to submit comparisons for benchmark pricing, to prove that they’re not violating rules and exploiting customers. The issue is what kind of businesses are considered comparable for the purposes of “street pricing.”.

For example, 9NEWS recently investigated this at Denver Airport, finding that a basic Starbucks coffee cost $4.55 in the airport, compared to $2.95 outside the airport (a 54% markup), and a bag of cashews cost $9.99 in the airport, compared to $4.74 outside the airport (a 110% markup).

The airport’s VP of Concessions agreed to sit down with the reporter to discuss this, and she said the results of his investigation were great news — she suggested that 93% of the prices were compliant, and said “that’s pretty darn good.” How could that be, given the high markups compared to nearby businesses?

The problem boils down to how much latitude businesses have to submit pricing comparisons:.

What’s wild is how the airport official responds to Starbucks just having consistent pricing, and violating the rules:.

Recent findings suggest that VP of Concessions: “What I get from that is, they’re looking for consistency, across the board, across the nation, across the world.”Reporter: “I can’t help but think that travelers may be looking for consistency, but if they see a cheaper cup of coffee, they’ll probably be okay with it.”VP of Concessions: “I don’t know the answer to that. This is how we take care of our passengers, by ensuring that they are paying fair and transparent pricing, while supporting our business partners.”.

Back to the original story, the More Perfect Union reporter confronted the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey about pricing like $6.89 for one liter of Smart Water, compared to closer to $3.50 at nearby bodegas.

The response was that “comparing a Hudson to a bodega isn’t appropriate,” because “Hudson is a specialty market.” The approved price comparison was reportedly based on the price of water at Tablet Works, a “wellness & concierge pharmacy” in a high-end mall.

Sources indicate that the other thing to keep in mind is that a large percentage of airport retailers and restaurants are run by the same few companies, like HMSHost, which is a subsidiary of Avolta. So clearly they have a centralized approach to submitting pricing comparisons, and know exactly what they’re doing. Interestingly, the few independent businesses in some airports were found to have the most honest pricing.

Recent findings suggest that so to sum it up, the system is designed to be rigged. Airport authorities can technically pretend they’re looking out for consumers by setting a cap. Retailers can submit pricing comparisons to the highest prices they can find anywhere. Then airport authorities verify those prices to pretend they’re doing their jobs.

Airports are obviously complicit in all of this. They make money by charging sky high rent, and the reason they can do that is because retailers can charge hugely inflated prices. The more profits retailers make, the more airports can charge in rent. And they know that no consumer is going to avoid an airport because of high concession costs.

Around 80% of airports in the United States cap the prices that retailers can charge, so in most cases, you’re not supposed to be paying more than 15% above “street pricing.” The matter is the liberties that businesses can take with what constitutes “street pricing.”.

The price of the bottle of water or smoothie you’re buying isn’t compared to what you’d pay at a nearby gas station and smoothie shop, but instead, is being compared to what you’d pay at Erewhon. Talk about a very broken system, with no incentives for any party to actually be honest….

Iraqi Airways Is Selling Saddam Hussein’s 2 Boeing 747s After 35 Years In The Desert

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (634 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, iraqi Airways is looking for buyers for two Boeing 747s that have been grounded since the Gulf War in 1991.
  • The jets have been parked for longer than they were in service, with the jets initially grounded to keep them safe in the Gulf War.
  • While these jets have been idle, the sales team at Iraqi Airways has not.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, iraqi Airways is looking for buyers for two Boeing 747s that have been grounded since the Gulf War in 1991. The planes, once in the service of Saddam Hussein, have been sitting in the Tunisian desert at Tozeur-Nefta International Airport (TOE) since then.

The jets have been parked for longer than they were in service, with the jets initially grounded to keep them safe in the Gulf War. It isn't known if these jets are airworthy or how much work would be needed.

While these jets have been idle, the sales team at Iraqi Airways has not. The planes, a 747-200 (YI-AGP) and a 747SP (YI-ALM), have been up for sale before, without any luck. The first attempt was made in 2010. During the second sales attempt in 2023, the jets were valued at $494,000 each. AeroTelegraph reports they are listed at $900,000 each, meaning the jets cost less than some latest hypercars. What has changed to nearly double the jets' value is not clear. There is also flexibility, as prospective buyers can purchase one or both of the aircraft.

The Iraqi Embassy in Tunisia is acting as the broker for the sale. It thinks a deal can be completed before January 7, 2027. It may need to be even more flexible on pricing to sell the aircraft in such a short time. Yet, Iraqi Airways has refused to confirm whether the jets are airworthy.

Recent findings suggest that whoever buys them will need to invest a lot of money if they have looks to fly the aircraft. They will also have to deal with the plane's transport, storage, customs paperwork, and other associated costs.

The jets came to Tunisia in the early 1990s to protect them during Operation Desert Storm, which saw much of Iraq's aviation capabilities bombed to oblivion. 35 years later, the planes are still stored at TOE at monumental expense to the Iraqi government.

In 2020, aeroTELEGRAPH reported that the Iraqi government and the TOE airport authorities had signed a deal for a payment of approximately $5.4 million in parking fees and other outstanding charges. It isn't known what other payments Iraq may have made to the airport or the Tunisian government over the three decades.

Tunisia supported Iraq in the period around the Gulf War, refusing to attend the 1990 Cairo Summit at which nations voted to condemn Saddam's regime and the Iraqi state. The initial storage agreement may have been a gesture of goodwill or part of another diplomatic arrangement. When the jets arrived in Tunisia, they were painted white to remove the Iraqi Airlines livery. In 2012, reports from Tunisia suggested that the harsh desert conditions had begun to strip away the paint, and that the old green livery was starting to show, MiG Flug has revealed.

In a recent development, the Gulf War did not last long, but the 747s could not go home. This was because of an international embargo, parking charges, and a lawsuit, the latter of which was the most significant. Kuwait Airways Corporation sued Iraq and Iraqi Airways in London because 10 airliners with Iraqi Airways crews had flown out of Kuwait after the invasion. Kuwait Airways remarked this amounted to theft and demanded $1.8 billion for the jets and the spare parts inventory loaded onto them.

Six of these aircraft were in Iran for safekeeping. The remaining four jets were destroyed during Mosul air raids. The case became the English Commercial Court's longest ever. It led to a worldwide freezing order being made against Iraqi Airways, preventing the 747s from flying back to Iraq.

The case was finally settled in 2012. Iraqi Airways agreed to pay Kuwait Airways $500 million, far less than Kuwait Airways claimed the stolen inventory and jets were worth.

Emirates is known for being a world-class airline, though at this point, the carrier’s ground experience at Dubai International Airport (DXB) leaves a lot to be desired, especially for premium passengers.

In a recent development, while I don’t want to suggest that the carrier’s first class lounges and business class lounges are terrible, they’re far from cutting edge, and the design definitely feels extremely outdated. Earlier this year, I wrote a post asking if Emirates was going to revamp its lounges at the airport, or just wait until the theoretical move to Dubai World Central (DWC) around 2032.

Recent findings suggest that well, it seems that my concerns have now been addressed, as Emirates has revealed plans to completely transform its lounge experience in Dubai. Over the summer we saw the airline start to roll out a newly introduced global lounge concept for outstation lounges, and that idea is now coming to Dubai as well.

Sources indicate that as is the case for any airline, rolling out a fresh lounge concept at a hub airport isn’t easy, given that it requires spaces to be closed. So that’s why it’s worth noting that Emirates is taking an innovative approach to refreshing its lounges in Dubai:.

Emirates is investing a total of 400 million AED ($109 million) in these lounge spaces. Interestingly, Emirates claims that “all flagship lounges” will be getting a redesign, though there’s zero mention of the lounges in Concourse A, which are the biggest lounges in the world (they span the entire concourse), and offer direct boarding to planes. So it’s not clear when those lounges will undergo updates.

Here’s how Emirates President Tim Clark describes this development:.

“Our customers expect the very best from Emirates, whether while flying or spending time with us on the ground. We believe the airport experience should be every bit as exceptional as the journey itself, and that’s why we are transforming our lounges globally. This upcoming First Class Lounge in Dubai is the first taste of what’s to come. And if these are the lengths we will go to for a temporary lounge… just imagine what you can expect from new Emirates Lounges going forward. Over the next two years, we’ll be unveiling a completely different lounge experience, with new concepts in dining, wellness, entertainment and personalised hospitality. We’re going well beyond a traditional refurbishment and creating extraordinary spaces.”.

We’ve already seen how Emirates is overhauling its global lounge network, and I’d say the changes are pretty awesome. So what can we expect in Dubai? As you can see, Clark references how the temporary latest first class lounge is just a small glimpse into what we can expect in the future. Below is a video showing the new concept, and I must say, it looks impressive!

Here’s how Emirates describes the lounge concept, broadly:.

Featuring immersive culinary experiences to dedicated wellness facilities and innovative entertainment concepts, Emirates is redefining what customers can expect from their time at the airport. Building on Emirates’ renowned hospitality, customers can expect distinct spaces for dining, relaxation, work and socialising – complemented by intuitive technology, refined interiors and elevated personal service. Each lounge will bear the hallmarks of the iconic Emirates brand, with the interiors conveying luxury, comfort, exceptional hospitality and global appeal.

When it comes to the temporary latest first class lounge, here are the details:.

As much as people like to suggest that Gulf carriers just throw money down the drain when it comes to passenger experience, Emirates is actually a pretty disciplined and cost focused business, which is also clear based on the fact that the airline still has angled business class seats with seven seats per row. 😉.

But when the airline does invest and upgrade its products, it has a pretty good sense of what customers like. Barista coffee, Dom Perignon, and a gym? Count me in (though maybe the amenities shouldn’t be enjoyed in that order). 😉 It does sound like there still won’t be dedicated bedrooms, which would be disappointing, but also wouldn’t surprise me, given the volume of rooms they’d need to serve guests.

Two things stand out to me here:.

Emirates is hugely investing in its lounge network in Dubai, something that’s long overdue, if you ask me. Over the next two years, at least four lounges will be getting a full makeover, to match the carrier’s upcoming lounge aesthetic.

Sources indicate that we’ve just seen the opening of a new temporarily first class lounge in Concourse B, which is described as an example of what’s to come. Next year that lounge is expected to become a business class lounge, as a new flagship first class lounge opens, along with additional first and business class lounges.

In a recent development, the new design aesthetic looks great, and it sounds like some thought is being put into amenities as well. I look forward to seeing this transformation, though I can’t help but wonder if this reflects a delay with Emirates moving to its new hub airport.

  • In a recent development, so, what’s actually going on here?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, last Friday we saw the worst disruption to air travel that we’ve seen in the United States in over 25 years, as air traffic shut down nationwide for over four hours. We rapidly learned that this happened because L3Harris, a government contractor, was doing maintenance to switch telecommunications lines from copper to fiber.

The logical question is how something going wrong with the work of one contractor could cause our entire aviation ecosystem to shut down:.

In a recent development, so, what’s actually going on here? A newly introduced report sheds some more light on this….

CNN has some insights into how little oversight there was of the work being performed by FAA contractor L3Harris, which led to the ground stop disaster that we saw. When was oversight reduced? Well, in early 2025, coinciding with the FAA laying off a large number of employees, as part of Elon Musk’s “Department of Government Efficiency” (DOGE) stunt.

Recent findings suggest that according to this report, last Friday morning, an FAA technician escorted a contractor from L3Harris into a remote radio communications site for air traffic control in southern Arkansas, to replace a decades-old router. The FAA technician’s belief was that his role was done once the contractor entered the facility, according to people familiar with what happened, plus the union representing FAA employees.

That router replacement ended up being what triggered the communications challenges across the country, ultimately leading to the nationwide ground stop.

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford insists that the L3Harris engineer performing the upgrade “was monitored by an FAA technician” and that a risk assessment was performed, but sources dispute that characterization, pointing out that the technician “was only there to unlock the door,” and that “there was no monitoring.”.

Funny enough, an FAA spokesperson later contradicted Bedford, saying “the FAA escort is responsible for providing the L3Harris technician access to and from the building,” and “because it is L3 equipment, the escort is not there while the technician is doing work.” It’s amazing how they can’t even keep their narrative straight.

Industry observers note that this type of hands-off arrangement is apparently a recent development that happened under the Trump administration, and a change to how the FAA used to handle things. In March 2025, an FAA memo laid out changes to how FAA maintenance and upgrades would be carried out, in order to speed things up. The memo stated that “it is critical to approve maintenance performed by the Telecommunication Vendors without delay.”.

With this policy, the FAA also went from receiving maintenance “requests” from private contractors that needed to be approved, to receiving “notifications” of intended work, noting that “this work will proceed without FAA approval,” if not processed in time.

In a recent development, while the memo claimed that an FAA liaison will evaluate the “purpose, severity, criticality and impact” of the work, there are reportedly only a handful of liaisons nationwide, processing thousands of notifications. In this case, L3Harris reportedly submitted its “notification” with just a few days notice, meaning there was no meaningful oversight.

A spokesperson for the union representing FAA employees explains that “orders were to simply let the contractor in the building,” that he “had no direction to help or assist in any way,” and that “no PASS-represented employee was asked to conduct a risk assessment on this particular upgrade.”.

It also has to be pointed out that the March 2025 memo about a reduction in oversight came just weeks after Elon Musk’s DOGE laid off hundreds of FAA employees, making for the biggest single year layoffs at the organization in history.

That’s the beauty of slashing government inefficiency, right? If everything is working well, then we must not need all of those employees, eh? So to have a handful of people being “notified” of work and having to do an analysis sounds like it could be a problem.

We have to be honest, in general, politicians are really bad at accountability, and being honest when things go wrong. But whether you like Trump’s policies or not, there’s no denying that he takes lack of accountability to fresh levels. Everything good that happens is immediately his doing, and everything bad is Biden’s fault.

It would be nice if one Trump administration official actually had the introspection to say “hey, let’s make sure this doesn’t happen again,” rather than just yelling “give me $50 billion” and “Biden, Buttigieg, Biden, Buttigieg.”.

We’re getting a clearer picture of the circumstances that caused the nationwide ground stop last Friday, the biggest disruption to US air travel since 9/11. A contractor with L3Harris was given access to a site to replace wiring, with virtually no oversight from an FAA employee.

Sources indicate that while the FAA claims that there’s supposed to be oversight of contractor work, in this case the FAA employee was reportedly just tasked with unlocking the door. The approach to overseeing contractor work is reportedly a upcoming system as of March 2025, where contractor work went from being viewed as “requests” to being viewed as “notifications,” with just a handful of people to oversee these requests. This came just weeks after hundreds of employees were laid off from the FAA, thanks to Musk’s DOGE.

According to recent reports, ethan is an aviation professional with a degree in Aviation Management with Flight from the Florida Institute of Technology. He previously wrote aviation and tourism features for Florida Tech’s student newspaper, The Crimson, where he developed a clear, reader‑focused reporting style. Aviation journalism has remained a consistent priority throughout his career.

He presently holds a Restricted ATP and Commercial Multi‑Engine Pilot certificate and works in aviation supply chain and aircraft component repair. Alongside his industry role, he is pursuing his Certified Flight Instructor rating and actively building flight experience.

A lifelong aviation enthusiast, Ethan spent countless hours at Raleigh–Durham International Airport’s observation deck studying air traffic and practicing amateur photography and videography.

Chartering aircraft has been a popular alternative to commercial air travel since the end of World War II, according to Business Aircraft Center. The introduction of the Learjet 23 in 1963 further cemented charter aircraft operations as a mainstay in the corporate aviation landscape. Several manufacturers from the 1960s onward began to produce their own variants, to grow the business aviation landscape as it stands today. Companies such as Bombardier, Dassault Falcon, Gulfstream, Embraer, and Textron are some of the most common corporate jet manufacturers in the industry today.

However, many customers looking to pursue an aircraft charter, rather than a commercial ticket, may opt for something larger. A Hawker 400XP, for example, typically only has capacity for 6–8 passengers, according to Textron. Some missions require a substantially larger aircraft. Airbus Corporate Jets (ACJ) and Boeing Business Jets (BBJ) are the next step-up. These programs offer customers a larger cabin in the Airbus A319 or Boeing 737, configured to carry 100 passengers or more.

Industry observers note that what if a 737 is still not major enough? Several companies offer even larger aircraft charters. Boeing 757, 767, and even 747 aircraft are available for charter on the open market from companies such asAtlas Air, Mercury Jets, Global Cargo Transport, orDelta Air Lines.

Chartering a Boeing 747 serves one core purpose: moving an unusually large number of people or an unusually large amount of cargo in a single, highly controlled, point‑to‑point operation. A Gulfstream G200, for example, may be an appropriate size for routine corporate aviation missions, such as executive employee transport, or even celebrity travel. But as soon as the mission involves a non-routine number of passengers, or an excessively heavy cargo load, aircraft such as the Boeing 747 become more relevant to charter.

From a cargo perspective, the 747’s design enables the transport of outsized or unusually dense freight that would exceed the structural or volumetric limits of mid‑size jets. The nose‑loading capability on certain variants further expands the types of cargo that can be accommodated, particularly in industrial, humanitarian, or government‑directed missions. These features make the aircraft a practical solution when the payload itself dictates the platform rather than the other way around.

Industry observers note that operational control is another factor that often drives the decision toward a 747 charter. Large‑scale movements such as corporate, military, or special event‑related each benefit from consolidating passengers or cargo into a single aircraft, reducing coordination complexity across multiple flights. In these cases, the 747’s scale becomes not just a convenience but an operational requirement.

Industry observers note that the Boeing 747 has historically been a valuable resource in transporting pilgrims to Hajj, the annual Islamic pilgrimage to Mecca, Saudi Arabia. Saudia, Garuda Indonesia, as well as specialized charter companies such as AK Charters of Türkiye, all offer a non-scheduled charter where a larger, densely configured aircraft like the Boeing 747 is the perfect tool. For such a trip, hundreds of pilgrims from around the world need to be transported to Saudi Arabia for several days, and then return home afterward. While regularly scheduled flights onboard a 747 from Jakarta Soekarno-Hatta International to Jeddah may not be economically viable, a charter allows companies to capitalize on such short-term demand without the economic investment of such a large-scale scheduled operation.

Another area where the Boeing 747 often makes an appearance in the charter landscape is in sports team transport. While sports teams typically opt for Boeing 737, 757, or Airbus A320 aircraft for away game charters, such matches played far from home sometimes require the extra range or capacity offered by the 747.

One of the most famous cases is the Latest Zealand All Blacks rugby team, who have repeatedly used Boeing 747‑400 charter flights for international tours and World Cup travel, according to The New Zealand Herald. NFL teams from the United States are also reported to use Boeing 747 aircraft as chartered equipment when playing away games abroad, such as in London or Dublin.

For example, the Montreal Canadiens charter an Air Canada Jetz A320 for their away game against the Los Angeles Kings. According to Airbus, the range for this aircraft type is between 3,300 to 3,500 nautical miles (6,111 to 6,482 km). The distance of this route is approximately 2,500 nautical miles (4,630 km), with more than enough margin for safety and alternate planning for dispatchers. However, according to the Los Angeles Times, the same Montreal team traveled to Stockholm, Sweden, for the 1990 Friendship Tour. This trip measures in at approximately 3,657 nautical miles (6,773 km), thus requiring equipment with longer range. Coupled with additional media personnel and training staff, the 747 on charter may have been the perfect choice for a non-routine event such as this.

According to recent reports, dubbed the "Houston Express" by The Points Guy, Atlas Air previously offered a charter service directly from Houston to Luanda, Angola due to the significance of both cities in the oil industry. The flight ended in 2018 due to decreased demand in the oil industry between the two regions, but served for 18 years from 2000-2018.

While not a seasonal demand spike, nor a sports-related need, this charter reveals another area where chartering a 747 may be useful: the corporate world. Aside from transporting CEOs and executives alone, the "Houston Express" proved that in some industries, a great proportion of the workforce needs to travel on a particular route. ExxonMobil and Chevron both have facilities in Houston and Angola. Because both companies employ thousands of people at each site, direct charter flights for these employees were a no-brainer.

Sources indicate that TAAG Angola Airlines looks on launching a latest US route between Angola and Houston, Texas by 2027. This would be the first resumption of nonstop services between the two cities since the "Houston Express" ended in 2018. The Boeing 787, with its economical fuel burn performance and stellar range, is an ideal equipment choice should TAAG successfully relaunch the route.

For 2025-2026, between several different brokers offering to liaise a 747 charter on the open market, the average hourly rate for such an operation in a passenger-configured aircraft is between $25,000 and $40,000, according to Jettly.

It has been revealed that the variant chosen is a key element that will impact price. Within the Boeing 747 family, charter customers can choose between the older 747-400 or the newer Boeing 747-8. The older variants offer higher overall maintenance costs. However, the newer, younger 747-8 has a higher hourly rate across the board. This is due to the ability for operators to configure newer aircraft with more state-of-the-art optional equipment. For example, only the newest airworthiness-certified cabin seats by a manufacturer like Safran can be applicable to the Boeing 747-8; not all fresh equipment is simply "plug and play" for older generation 747 models.

A one-way 747 charter between Fresh York and London typically costs $220,000 to $400,000, consisting of seven to nine billable hours plus taxes, landing fees, and positioning charges, with peak summer and holiday periods sitting at the high end. Two line items catch first-time charterers off guard. First, ferrying the aircraft to you: positioning (ferry) flights can add $25,000 to $75,000 per flight depending on where the aircraft is based, and billable time includes both airborne and positioning hours, according to Blade. Second, the ground costs unique to an aircraft this size: landing and handling fees that run $2,000 to $5,000 for a standard jet can easily reach $10,000 to $20,000 for a BBJ 747-8, on top of international permits, specialized ramp equipment, and per diem for a crew of two or three pilots and four or five cabin attendants.

For freight, the math is similar or steeper — a 747-400F freighter runs $30,000 to $50,000 per hour, with rates up 8–12% versus 2024 as operators retire 747Fs and shift to the more economical and scaled 777F.

Recent findings suggest that for freight operations, these hourly costs reflect not only fuel burn and crew requirements, but also the premium associated with wide‑body lift capacity. As 747‑400F availability tightens, charter clients increasingly face a supply‑driven pricing environment rather than a demand‑driven one. This dynamic makes the aircraft’s already high operating cost even more sensitive to market fluctuations.

It has been revealed that the transition toward the Boeing 777F further amplifies the pricing pressure on remaining 747‑400F operators. With fewer airframes in service, carriers can command higher rates for missions requiring nose‑loading or uniquely large volumetric capacity. As a result, shippers with oversized or non‑standard cargo often have little choice but to absorb these elevated charter costs.

The takeaway most brokers themselves stress is that a 747 only makes economic sense at genuine scale: for very large groups of 150 to 350 passengers on the same route, the per-seat cost can be comparable to or slightly above premium-cabin commercial fares — below that threshold, it's simply more aircraft than the mission needs.

The idea of chartering a 747 is a grandiose, extreme use case that only makes economic sense in a few key examples. Flights such as large, international sports team charters, Hajj flights, or dedicated corporate cargo or employee charters are common examples of when a Boeing 747 is the appropriate equipment for the mission.

Sources indicate that aside from the Boeing 747, the business aviation landscape offers prospective customers a wide variety of aircraft. More than likely, a smaller aircraft is suitable for the average business aviation customer; typically corporate executives, sports team managers, celebrities, and other high-net-worth individuals. Aircraft such as the Cessna CitationX, Gulfstream G550, or even Airbus ACJ provide the customer with enough variety and scale to appropriately align their specific needs. But the 747 is readily available to customers with extraordinary requirements that exceed normal payload.

Let me emphasize that the card will no longer offer a $99 companion fare, so that’s being replaced by the new 50% off vouchers that can be earned with spending.

As of November 18, 2026, customers who apply for a upcoming Atmos Rewards Business Card will be receiving the refreshed card, with the new benefits and fee.

What’s interesting is that current cardholders will keep their existing benefits, and will not be automatically moved over. However, you can call up Bank of America if you’d like to see about the opportunity of switching.

As of now, it sounds like there are no aims to transition people to the new system, so existing card members shouldn’t be negatively impacted by this.

The Atmos Rewards Business Card changes are a mixed bag. First, I want to once again emphasize that since existing card members aren’t impacted by these changes, I don’t think there should be too much frustration here.

Tech Report: Biden: ‘Hard to take’ as Pelosi, Schumer turned on him in 2024

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • President Joe Biden, Speaker Nancy Pelosi, and Senate Majority Leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y., arrive for The CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 bill signing at the White House, on Aug.
  • In conversations with Democratic strategists in recent months, I heard a strikingly similar sentiment when the topic turned to Joe Biden’s forthcoming memoir.
  • Spoiler alert: Biden offers only a full-throated defense of his decision to seek reelection in 2024, and expresses deep disappointment over what he casts as a disloyal pressure campaign orchestrated by party leaders to force him out of the presidential race despite what he cites as his successes in the office.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

President Joe Biden, Speaker Nancy Pelosi, and Senate Majority Leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y., arrive for The CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 bill signing at the White House, on Aug. 9, 2022. In his new memoir, Biden remarked he was disappointed when Pelosi and Schumer urged him to drop out of the presidential race in 2024. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

In conversations with Democratic strategists in recent months, I heard a strikingly similar sentiment when the topic turned to Joe Biden’s forthcoming memoir. The consensus view, even among some who’d worked for the former president, was that if he did anything other than accept some responsibility for his role in Donald Trump’s return to the White House, they didn’t have much appetite to hear what he had to say about anything else.

Spoiler alert: Biden offers only a full-throated defense of his decision to seek reelection in 2024, and expresses deep disappointment over what he casts as a disloyal pressure campaign orchestrated by party leaders to force him out of the presidential race despite what he cites as his successes in the office.

But while his perspective on the climactic moment of his political career will be the most scrutinized portion of Biden’s newly introduced book, “Promise Me, America” seems primarily intended to offer the former president a platform he has otherwise not had since leaving office: to catalog what he sees as his historic achievements and offer his perspective on how he wrestled with the major issues of our time.

Recent findings suggest that it’s often mentioned that the only thing better than being president is being a former president. That has hardly been the case for Biden in the nearly 22 months since he left the White House, especially as he’s endured what his son Hunter has described as “debilitating” physical pain following a cancer diagnosis last March.

But where “Thanks, Obama” became a popular mantra nearly a decade ago for Democrats seeking to defend and celebrate the 44th president’s record in contrast with the first Trump administration, no such widespread nostalgia has emerged around Biden, as the party is loath to revisit the trauma of the summer of 2024.

The sheer length of his upcoming book — more than 400 pages — seems an implicit acknowledgment that presenting a positive portrait of Biden’s single term in office is largely to be a solitary effort. Over 15 chapters, Biden offers sometimes mechanical descriptions of specific policies and their impact, but also new details of the sausage-making required to pass major initiatives like the Inflation Reduction Act. That legislation, he writes, was revived thanks in part to an Italian dinner hosted by Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo to make peace between West Virginia Sen. Joe Manchin III and White House Chief of Staff Ron Klain.

Biden writes in sweeping terms about other accomplishments like responding to the COVID-19 crisis he inherited, calling his administration’s work “one of the most monumental achievements in public health history.” He repeatedly defends his frequent efforts to warn Americans about the need to safeguard our democracy even as critics in the press and his own party suggested he focus more on economic concerns.

Supporting Ukraine in its war against Russia gets the most extensive treatment of any single issue in the book, including a detailed account of Biden’s clandestine trip to Kyiv in February 2023. And the former Senate Foreign Relations Committee chairman takes great effort to delve into the complexity of the U.S.-China relationship and his relationship with President Xi Jinping, while asserting that Taiwan “will likely be the most vital foreign policy challenge in the world over the next generation.”.

Recurring throughout the book are expressions of optimism that under his administration, Washington was beginning to work again like it was supposed to, that America’s global leadership was being restored through its alliances, and that he was tackling problems that previous presidents had sidestepped. And in offering this comprehensive presentation of his record, Biden also offers his primary rationale for running again.

“We had accomplished so much —  I wanted to finish the job. And yes: I believed I was the best person to do it,” he states. “I was the only person who had ever beaten Donald Trump. And I felt I was the best person to do it again.”.

One of Biden’s top advisers put it to me a different way in the months leading up to his decision to seek another term. “He has been running for president for 50 years. And the idea that he would actually be president and stop running for president is almost laughably preposterous.”.

The biggest question, of course, was his age, something Biden, who was 81 when he dropped out of the race, asserts he gave serious consideration.

In a recent development, “I knew better than anyone how old I was. I knew what I was —  and wasn’t —  capable of doing. I carefully monitored how I was meeting the demands of the job. And there is not a single example of me failing to handle my responsibilities,” he writes.

The June 27 debate, of course, created a very different perception, as Biden acknowledges that his flubbed comment that “we finally beat Medicare” was to become “Exhibit A that I was too old to do the job.” But he tries to argue it was no different than the poor showings of previous incumbent presidents, including President Barack Obama, in their first debates.

“The difference was that every other president was given the chance to redeem themselves in a second debate. As it turned out, that chance would not be available to me,” Biden writes.

He argues the response he was seeing from voters at his public events after the debate didn’t justify the panicked response of elected Democrats in Washington, and that public polling revealed only minor slippage after the debate, until a steady drumbeat of elected Democrats publicly began calling for him to step aside.

Describing separate visits from former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and then-Senate Majority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., personally urging him to step aside, he says there was a “yawning gap between what I was seeing with Democratic voters and what I was hearing from the Democratic leadership in Washington.”.

Industry observers note that “I have to admit it was personally hard to take so many old friends turning on me,” Biden states. “I told Schumer he had a lot of gumption (I may have said it differently at the time), coming to my home and telling me to get out of the race. Loyalty matters to me. If I give you my word, I stick with you. If I say I’m with you, I’m with you to the end.”.

At one point, Biden seems to reflect some resentment that some of the Democrats who would ultimately call on him to drop out of the race had themselves been too afraid to challenge him in the first place, saying: “Anyone who was scared off from running has no business being president.” While there was a constant narrative about the weakness of his candidacy, Biden acknowledges, the lack of a serious challenger was in fact a sign of his strength.

Industry observers note that “I had it on good authority that several substantial names in Democratic politics had looked at running. They held meetings and took polls and talked to donors and to potential staff. If they thought I was weak or vulnerable, they would have taken their shot. But they didn’t,” he writes.

In a recent development, biden’s defiant tone, and his insistence that the lack of party unity was a greater threat to his continued candidacy than his own performance, may be dismissed by Democrats who don’t want to revisit this difficult chapter. But as Schumer and other Democratic leaders are now facing their own internal challenges, “Promise Me, America” may also serve as a cautionary note for an ambitious crop of potential candidates hoping to reclaim the presidency in 2028.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After a three-year hiatus, American Airlines is preparing to resume service to Israel.

In a recent development, the carrier said Friday that it will restart flights from Upcoming York-JFK to Tel Aviv on March 27, 2027. Flights will operate daily using Boeing 777-200ER aircraft.

American has not flown to Israel since the Hamas attack on southern Israel in October 2023. It remained on the sidelines even as rivals United and Delta resumed service to Ben Gurion International Airport, though they too were forced to temporarily pause flights during fighting between Israel and Iran.

In a recent development, israeli officials had questioned why American was slow to reconnect the country, citing the importance of air links between Tel Aviv and Latest York. The airline did not offer an explanation beyond concern for the safety of its passengers and crew.

Industry observers note that american also said Friday that it has formed a commercial partnership with Tel Aviv-based low-cost carrier Israir. The agreement will expand in phases over time, American said; in the first phase, Israir will place its code on American’s flights between JFK and Tel Aviv.

The carriers will also work to implement an interline agreement that would give Israir customers access to American’s network across the U.S., Canada, Latin America, and the Caribbean from JFK.

According to recent reports, “American looks forward to building a relationship with Israir that will give customers the convenient, well-connected travel options they desire,” American Senior Vice President of Alliances Anmol Bhargava stated in a news release. “As we prepare to resume service between New York and Tel Aviv next spring, this partnership will help us deliver a stronger customer proposition in the market and create more opportunities for Israir’s travelers to connect beyond our JFK gateway.”.

Industry observers note that israir operates five weekly flights between JFK and Tel Aviv using Airbus A330-200 aircraft. Latest York is its only U.S. destination; most of its network is concentrated in the Near East and Europe.

Industry observers note that I use aeroplan a lot from Australia. Lot of air India. Quite a lot of Thai airways. Some ANA. Limited Turkish. No Ethiopian or United anymore sadly. Occasionally some Singapore economy redemptions that tack on to long haul Thai biz flights. Some asiana but mostly economy. Still valuable close in. 52.5k points to Asia in biz. Ironically found more confirmed availability on lifemiles when searching this week from Sydney to Asia. Def has value when searching for 1-2 people close in at this price. Just my opinion based on being in Sydney.

If we're going to talk about partners, we have to talk about how availability keeps getting worse and worse.

Too many blocked partners. Change and cancel fees way too high. I guess if you like redeeming on Air India, or worse AC metal at 500k, then maybe yes worth it?

Ben, perfect time for you to post this - I've been trying to transfer AMEX MR points to Aeroplan for over 36h, with no success. They will show as deducted from my AMEX account, but within a relatively short time reappear. They never show up in my Aeroplan account. Is anyone else having concerns? #19445. Why America’s Most Controversial Overseas Military Base Sits In Legal Limbo

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1937 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

Why America’s Most Controversial Overseas Military Base Sits In Legal Limbo

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1937 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that one of America’s most key bomber bases sits on an island the United States has never owned, that the world’s highest court notes Britain should have returned, and whose future now hangs on a treaty that has been signed but cannot take effect.
  • That creates a problem far bigger than a dispute over a line on a map.
  • Recent findings suggest that the story starts with a map redrawn at the last minute.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that one of America’s most key bomber bases sits on an island the United States has never owned, that the world’s highest court notes Britain should have returned, and whose future now hangs on a treaty that has been signed but cannot take effect. Diego Garcia is a coral atoll in the Indian Ocean with a runway of roughly 12,000 feet (3,659 meters), according to SKYbrary. Few overseas airfields matter more to American long-range airpower. Few stand on shakier legal ground.

That creates a problem far bigger than a dispute over a line on a map. Britain, Mauritius, the displaced Chagossians and Washington each have competing interests in Diego Garcia, but the most important question for the US military is much more practical: can America be certain it will still have unrestricted access to one of its most strategically useful bomber bases? The answer depends on a treaty signed in 2025, an agreement dating back to 1966, and a dispute that has yet to be resolved.

Recent findings suggest that the story starts with a map redrawn at the last minute. According to Al Jazeera, Britain separated the Chagos Archipelago from Mauritius in 1965, three years before Mauritian independence, and later built a base with the United States on Diego Garcia, the largest island. Between 1968 and 1973, as the same report notes, authorities removed an estimated 1,400 to 1,700 Chagossians. Many ended up in Mauritius and the Seychelles, and returning without permission became illegal. The human cost still echoes: Olivier Bancoult of the Chagos Refugees Group told Al Jazeera that mourners at one funeral scattered sand from Chagos into an elder’s tomb, honoring his unfulfilled wish to die in his homeland.

Chatham House explains that the 1965 separation was agreed at a London conference in exchange for £3 million, after which the UK created the British Indian Ocean Territory and kept it out of Mauritius’s independence. In 2019, the International Court of Justice advised that the separation was unlawful and that the UK should end its administration as rapidly as possible. The opinion is not legally binding, Chatham House stresses, but the UN General Assembly endorsed it. Critical Legal Thinking adds that the Court’s vote was thirteen to one, and that Britain let the UN’s six-month deadline pass. The dispute therefore became more than a question of colonial history: Britain was still administering the territory containing an active US military base, making the future of Diego Garcia inseparable from the sovereignty dispute.

According to recent reports, negotiations followed instead, and in May 2025, London and Port Louis signed a treaty. That raises an awkward puzzle: if the deal hands sovereignty to Mauritius, why was it sold as a way to protect the base?

Signed on May 22, 2025, the treaty would let Mauritius exercise sovereignty over the whole archipelago while the UK keeps rights over Diego Garcia for an initial 99 years, as reported by Al Jazeera. For the US military, that distinction is critical: Mauritius would gain sovereignty, but the arrangement is designed to preserve continued British and American use of the airbase. Chatham House says the lease can be extended. Critical Legal Thinking puts the extension at 40 years, lists payments of £165 million a year for three years, then £120 million a year, and says the British Indian Ocean Territory would cease to exist as a legal entity. It also describes a 24-nautical-mile (about 28 miles, or 44 km) buffer zone where nothing can be built without UK consent.

For Chagossians, the deal opens only part of the door. Resettlement is allowed on islands other than Diego Garcia, but UN Special Rapporteurs observed in June 2025, as Critical Legal Thinking recounts, that the agreement was reached without Chagossian consent. Why do a lease and a buffer zone matter so much? Because of what flies from there. As Simple Flying reports, the Northrop B-2 Spirit has an unrefueled range of about 6,000 nautical miles (11,112 km), and crews have flown missions lasting more than 40 hours. Meanwhile, Simple Flying’s analysis of the B-52 notes that the veteran bomber can carry up to 70,000 lb (32,000 kg) of mixed ordnance. Both types need a runway and a legal right to use it.

Mauritius, over the whole archipelago.

£165 million a year for 3 years, then £120 million a year.

24 nautical miles (about 28 miles / 44 km).

Outer islands only, not Diego Garcia.

Sources indicate that but a treaty only works if the other treaty, the older one, lets it. And the older one contains a sentence that has now become the most argued-over line in the dispute.

That older paper is the 1966 US-UK agreement governing the American military presence on Diego Garcia. Chatham House describes it as granting extensive basing rights for an initial 50 years, renewing automatically for 20 more, to 2036. Its first clause notes the territory remains under UK sovereignty. That wording is now at the heart of the dispute because the 2025 treaty would transfer sovereignty to Mauritius while preserving the military arrangement. The pause in Lords debate followed a Conservative amendment claiming that ratification would breach the 1966 agreement. For Washington, the glitch is therefore not simply who owns Diego Garcia, but whether the legal framework supporting American access to the airbase can survive the change.

It has been revealed that experts disagree sharply. The Chatham House analysis argues that the clause was written to reassure London, not to bind it forever, noting that either side can terminate the arrangement with two years’ notice. It also points out that Secretary of State Marco Rubio publicly welcomed the 2025 deal, which, in its view, cost Washington any right to object. The Mauritius Times sees a tighter bind: the 1966 notes do not override the new treaty under UK law, but they stop London from finalizing a transfer without American consent, leaving what it calls a legal deadlock.

Both readings point to the same hinge: a formal exchange of letters from Washington. Which raises the obvious question. Why would the United States risk so much over one island?

It has been revealed that because few places can do what Diego Garcia does. Simple Flying explains that overseas hubs such as Diego Garcia and RAF Fairford regularly host American bombers, but typically support only one bomber type per deployment. It adds that few foreign bases can sustain B-2 operations for long, because stealth coatings are sensitive to humidity and contamination, so each deployment is a carefully planned logistics exercise. In other words, the base is only as dependable as the legal right to use it.

The base also has a political cost because its military role is inseparable from the sovereignty dispute. Al Jazeera reports that Mauritius has stated that strikes released from Diego Garcia against Iran breached international law. International relations consultant Bruno Donat argues the treaty could give Mauritius more leverage over how the base is used. The Mauritian group Lalit wants the base closed entirely; its spokesperson, Lindsey Collen, warns that Mauritius might become a target if its land is used this way.

Chagossian leader Olivier Bancoult says his community is opposed to war but is running out of time. That leaves Washington facing a difficult calculation: preserving access to the base is strategically valuable, but its future use is becoming increasingly tied to the political and legal terms under which Mauritius accepts the arrangement. With stakes that high, a frozen treaty is not a small bureaucratic hiccup. So who pulled the brake, and when?

Washington’s tone shifted in stages. Chatham House notes that by February 2025, President Trump seemed “inclined” to back the arrangement. By January 2026, Al Jazeera reports, he was criticizing it harshly and questioning whether it protected the base. In the same month, per Critical Legal Thinking, the House of Lords added amendments requiring a Chagossian referendum and the suspension of payments if the base became militarily inoperable. Weeks later, the Trump administration withdrew support and refused the exchange of letters needed to amend the 1966 treaty.

The Mauritius Times says the UK placed the handover in a “deep freeze” as of April 15, 2026, and Al Jazeera adds that the government told Parliament the bill could not finish its passage before the session ended on April 29. Critical Legal Thinking says the bill was paused with no plans to reintroduce it, although the Mauritius Times notes that London still says it is engaging with both capitals and considers the treaty the best way to secure the base’s long-term future. Meanwhile, the Mauritius Times notes that the territory’s administration paused upcoming visitor-permit applications for the outer islands on March 31.

It has been revealed that however, the story did not end in April. In September, the UK and Mauritius returned to discussions, with Burnham saying he wanted to work with Mauritius and the United States on a solution that would secure the continued operation of Diego Garcia and protect national security.

Industry observers note that by November, the discussions had moved beyond simply trying to revive the stalled treaty. Burnham stated Britain was talking to Washington about how to “recast” the arrangement so it better addressed American concerns, describing Diego Garcia as a priority because of its strategic significance. He also suggested that the recently negotiated Greenland arrangement between the US and Denmark might offer a model for finding a solution.

It has been revealed that according to Al Jazeera, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham mentioned on September 21 that the UK would work with Mauritius and the US on a way forward that secures the base. Five days later, Mauritian Prime Minister Navin Ramgoolam flew to London to meet National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell. Mauritius, for its part, still calls its sovereignty non-negotiable, while sharing little about the substance of the talks. Donat argues Mauritius should keep engaging the African Union, small island states, the Commonwealth Secretariat, and sympathetic US lawmakers to build pressure on Washington. In June, Al Jazeera adds, Chagos Refugees Group members traveled to the UK to lobby every major party except Reform UK.

The test is simple to state and hard to pass: will Washington send the letters? If not, the Mauritius Times notes, Mauritius has threatened to sue the UK for financial loss, though London states there are no legal grounds. Time is also a factor, since Al Jazeera says Chagossians born on the islands are now between 53 and 100 years old. Even they are divided: some, led by UK-based Misley Mandarin, favor resettlement under British sovereignty.

It has been revealed that for the US military, however, the question ultimately comes back to the runway. Diego Garcia's value does not come from the legal status of a line on a map, but from what that isolated airfield allows American aircraft to do. B-2s and B-52s can use it as a long-range operating hub in a part of the world where equivalent alternatives are limited. That makes the future of the base a strategic aviation question as much as a diplomatic one.

According to recent reports, critical Legal Thinking offers a blunt verdict: where the base goes, sovereignty bends. For a visual primer, Wendover Productions explores the dispute in its October 2026 video, America’s Most Illegal Military Base. But the unresolved question is no longer simply who owns Diego Garcia. It is whether the United States, Britain, and Mauritius can create a legal framework stable enough to keep one of America's most key overseas airbases operating for decades to come.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Rove has grown quickly since launching in 2025, expanding to 22 airline and hotel transfer partners.
  • Online shopping portals and card-linked merchant offers are some of the best ways to earn additional rewards on top of what you earn from your credit card.
  • Here's what you should know about Rove's new offerings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rove has grown quickly since launching in 2025, expanding to 22 airline and hotel transfer partners. Now, just in time for the holiday shopping season, Rove has rolled out personalized shopping offers that let members earn up to 25 Rove miles per dollar on select purchases. The program has also expanded its in-store shopping offers.

Online shopping portals and card-linked merchant offers are some of the best ways to earn additional rewards on top of what you earn from your credit card. TPG's November 2026 valuations peg Rove miles at 2.05 cents apiece, so earning 25 Rove miles per dollar could yield rewards of up to 51.25 cents per dollar spent.

Here's what you should know about Rove's new offerings.

Rove members already know they can navigate to the shopping tab on the Rove website or app and see featured offers or search for a specific merchant.

Now, Rove members who link and connect an eligible payment card can access personalized offers in the For You section of Rove's website and app.

Industry observers note that when a personalized offer has a higher earning rate than Rove's standard offer, you'll see both rates displayed. Since these offers are personalized, the available merchants and earning rates may vary by member. Plus, a Rove spokesperson told TPG that Rove refreshes its offers each week, so you may see latest or different offers the next time you check.

You'll need to activate each offer before making a qualifying purchase. Click the plus button to activate, and then check the circle that replaces the plus after activation to see how long you have to use the offer.

Be sure to review each offer's terms before purchasing, including where the offer is valid, when it expires and whether any spending limits or purchase exclusions apply.

Sources indicate that by reviewing the Hyatt House and Hyatt Studios offer I enrolled in, I found it is only valid for stays within the U.S. This is too bad, as I was excited to use it for an upcoming Hyatt House stay in Canada until I read its terms.

Finally, it's worth noting that neither TPG's Lyndsey Matthews nor I saw any offers in our For You sections for 25 miles per dollar spent. Instead, 15 miles per dollar spent on a new Sam's Club membership purchase is the best offer either of us found in our accounts.

Related: Why the holiday season is the best time to start earning points and miles.

In a recent development, rove initially introduced in-store card-linked offers in August. It now indicates members can earn miles on qualifying purchases at hundreds of participating physical retailers.

To earn Rove miles on an in-store purchase, link an eligible card to Rove and review the merchant's offer before making a purchase. Activate the offer first if required, then use your linked card to make a qualifying purchase. Rove states transactions are automatically tracked after the charge clears and that miles typically post within seven days.

Related: 5 tips to maximize rewards and avoid debt this holiday shopping season.

Rove's personalized offers could be a lucrative way to earn transferable rewards on purchases you already planned to make, especially when targeted rates reach 25 miles per dollar.

Sources indicate that however, offers and earning rates will vary by member, so check the For You section and review the activation and purchase requirements before shopping. You should also compare Rove's rate with other shopping portals and check for card-linked merchant offers you may be able to stack with your purchase.

Recent findings suggest that based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Atmos Rewards points to be worth 1.5 cents each, meaning the 90,000 points are worth $1,350 to me, which is among the best bonuses out there. There are lots of great uses of Atmos Rewards points, for travel on Alaska, Hawaiian, oneworld partners, and non-alliance partners.

In a recent development, atmos Rewards points have all kinds of uses, ranging from booking short haul one-way economy awards on American for 4,500 points, to booking Starlux business class one-way awards from the US to Asia for 75,000 points. How do the previous Atmos Rewards Business Card bonuses compare?

In a recent development, as you can see, the Atmos Rewards Business Card sign-up bonus has varied from 70,000 points to 90,000 points, and the current bonus of 90,000 points is the best publicly available offer we’ve seen. So if there has ever been a time to apply for this card, this is it.

When it comes to getting approved for the Atmos Rewards Business Card, what rules should you be aware of? There are the card specific policies, and then also the more generic Bank of America policies. When you pull up the application, you’ll see the following terms:.

The Atmos Rewards Business Card has introduced a best-ever welcome offer, whereby you can earn 90,000 Atmos Rewards points upon completing minimum spending.

This is an exceptional bonus, and this card is absolutely worth picking up for the points, especially given that eligibility isn’t mutually exclusive with other Atmos Rewards cards. In the long run, the card can be worth it for the perks for travel on Alaska and Hawaiian.

Anecdotally I find Bank of America business cards to be quite easy to get approved for, including if you’ve had the card in the past. Applying for this card also shouldn’t count as a further card toward the Chase 5/24 limit, if that’s of concern to you.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    There’s still quite a gender gap in the airline industry, with a disproportionate number of pilots being male, and a disproportionate number of flight attendants being female. Airlines will sometimes have special celebrations with all-female crews, so here’s an interesting twist on that.

    Industry observers note that today is (apparently) International Men’s Day. We often see airlines commemorate International Women’s Day, but there aren’t many airlines that celebrate the equivalent for men… well, except Finnair! The airline has today operated its annual flight with an all-male crew. This was the case for Finnair flight AY1331, from Helsinki (HEL) to London (LHR), using an Airbus A350-900.

    In a recent development, the crew consisted of 10 people, comprised of two pilots and eight flight attendants. The gate agents were also all men. So, why is this vital? Finnair highlights how only around 10% of cabin crew at the airline are male, but the firm hopes to see that number grow in the future.

    I think this is a fun concept, and it would be nice to see a closer to 50/50 gender ratio in both the cockpit and cabin, as it would show that everyone is given a fair chance at such a career.

    Sources indicate that I think it’s worth acknowledging that at many airlines, hiring of flight attendants is still primarily or exclusively based on gender. Now, the policies do vary significantly by airline, but perhaps an extreme example is India’s largest airline, IndiGo, which only hires female flight attendants. It’s literally written on the application, that it’s a job for “Female Indian nationals.”.

    It’s all so strange, because the airline has this super enthusiastic page about the importance of diversity in the workplace, and says “all employment decisions are made solely on the basis of merit and qualifications, without regard to a candidate’s gender…” You mean except the single largest portion of your workforce, which is cabin crew?

    What’s interesting is that while those gender restrictions exist in the cabin, roughly 18% of the carrier’s pilots are female, which is way above the global average of 7%. That’s obviously a conscious effort, so I guess the idea is that women can become pilots but men can’t become flight attendants.

    In fairness, I suspect part of the motivation here is that IndiGo flight attendants share hotel rooms on layovers, and that is a bit more complicated with mixed genders. Then again, it seems easy enough to just try to pair male flight attendants on trips, so it’s hardly a hurdle that can’t be overcome.

    Recent findings suggest that while we’re used to seeing airlines celebrate International Women’s Day, it’s rare to see an airline celebrating International Men’s Day. Finnair has operated an all-male flight today, intended to highlight how only 10% of flight attendants at the airline are male, and the airline wants to change that. While an unconventional initiative nowadays, I think this is still pretty cool.
