    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that rep. Gabe Evans, here arriving at the Capitol in July for a House Republican Conference meeting, lost his bid for a second term representing Colorado's 8th District. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

    Colorado Rep. Gabe Evans, who lost reelection earlier this month, declared Monday a 2028 run from the neighboring district of fellow defeated Republican Rep. Lauren Boebert.

    “Now more than ever, Colorado needs conservatives in Congress who will fight to keep our border secure, cut taxes for working families, keep boys from dominating girls' sports and locker rooms, protect our water, and make energy affordable,” Evans mentioned in a statement.

    Industry observers note that his announcement comes less than two weeks after he lost his bid for a second term representing the battleground 8th District in the Denver area. While the race had been considered one of the most competitive in the country, Democratic former state Rep. Manny Rutinel secured victory by 15 points.

    Sources indicate that as part of House Democrats’ massive midterm gains, they flipped three seats in Colorado. Boebert narrowly lost her reelection bid in the 4th District to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, while Republican Rep. Jeff Crank lost in the 5th District.

    Evans’ statement cited his ties to the 4th District, which encompasses the eastern part of the state and extends into the Denver metro area.

    “From Loveland to Lamar, I’m ready to keep fighting in the 4th District, where I grew up, and where my family has lived since 1976,” he mentioned.

    The district has a deep history of voting Republican. Boebert won by 11 points in 2024 while Donald Trump carried the district by 18 points.

    Evans is far from the first member of Congress to switch to a district seen as more favorable to his party. Boebert herself shifted from Colorado's more competitive 3rd District to run for the heavily conservative 4th in 2024.

    The 4th District will likely be a top target for Republicans in 2028, and Evans’ campaign sought to portray him as a clear front-runner in what could become a crowded GOP primary.

    In a recent development, “Gabe Evans will enter 2027 and the race for Colorado’s 4th Congressional District with $300,000 in campaign funds and name recognition that no first-time candidate in the district could match,” his campaign said in the statement. “Combined with his record as an Army aviator, police officer, rancher, and member of Congress, that gives him a head start in money, name recognition, and credibility before the field takes shape.”.

    Industry observers note that A former state legislator and Denver-area police officer, Evans also served 12 years in the Army. He was first elected to the House in 2024, unseating Democrat Yadira Caraveo, and right now sits on the Energy and Commerce and Homeland Security committees.

    Industry observers note that laubacher, a Navy veteran who will take office on Jan. 3, is the first Democrat elected to represent the 4th District since Betsy Markey won her lone term in 2008. In response to Evans’ announcement, Laubacher’s campaign said she would be “focused on making Washington deliver” for district residents.

    “There’s real work to do: ending the war in Iran that Gabe Evans voted six times to continue, lowering the cost of groceries and fertilizer that his eight votes for the tariffs helped drive up, and protecting the rural hospitals across the 4th district he voted to gut,” Laubacher spokesperson Taylor Gillespie remarked in a statement.

    Dad, here’s a blog post you should pay attention to (and thanks to Steve for flagging this)….

    It has been revealed that with banks, it’s typically possible to get your account statements by email or mail. There’s no denying that consumer preferences have shifted over the years, and along those lines, Amex has just sent an email to card members, informing them that “we’re making the switch to paperless.” Here’s the main part of the email:.

    We’re making the switch to paperless billing statements and account communications, beginning February 2027.

    Sources indicate that here’s what happens nextWe want to help you get ready to make the switch too. So, we’ve enrolled your account listed above in the paperless delivery option – but for now, we’ll continue to send you communications about your account in the mail. We’ll also mail your billing statements for the closing dates of November 2026, December 2026, and January 2027.

    After that, we’ll send account communications to you by email, and you’ll receive your monthly billing statements electronically. When they’re ready, you’ll be able to view them anytime by logging in to your account online at americanexpress.com or in the American Express App.

    Now, that makes it sound like people will be forced to switch to paperless billing, but I don’t believe that’s actually the case? Because further down in the email, it claims this:.

    Not ready to go paperless? No problem! You can re-enroll in paper billing statements and account communications by going to americanexpress.com/paperlesssettings, selecting “U.S. Mail,” and following the prompts to opt back in.

    So it seems like what’s happening here is that Amex will try to force everyone into paperless billing by making it the default, but maybe those who specifically once again state their preferences for paper billing will be able to maintain that communication method?

    Suffice it to say that going back 25 years, a vast majority of people got paper statements for their credit cards, while nowadays a vast majority of people get paperless statements, obviously reflecting the shift we’ve seen in how the internet is used.

    In a recent development, it’s funny, because I’m sure 99% of OMAAT readers would be confused at the thought of getting paper bills, and would wonder what purpose that serves. But then there are also people like my dad, who rely on paper statements for their credit cards, pay their statement by phone, etc.

    So it does sound like people will have the option of opting back into paper billing after being auto-enrolled in paperless billing, so the concept isn’t being eliminated altogether. Still, for my dad, there would likely be quite the learning curve.

    Sources indicate that then again, up until less than a decade ago he didn’t have a cell phone and insisted he didn’t need one, while now he kind of loves it, for everything from texting, to Googling all kinds of stuff. That’s of course a double-edged sword as well, because he seems to believe that if the Google AI summary states something, it must be true. We’re not talking things like vaccines. Instead, we’re talking things like whether the salmon at Red Lobster is good, etc. Anyway, I digress….

    As of February 2027, Amex will be automatically moving those with paper billing to paperless billing. While the message makes it sound like people will be forced to switch to paperless billing, that doesn’t seem to be the case, as Amex is also telling people they can once again enroll in paper billing statements and account communications if they’re “not ready to go paperless.” So Amex just seems to be trying to thin the ranks here of those using this feature.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    American Airlines is making another change to its senior leadership team, with Chief Operating Officer David Seymour set to retire at the end of the year.

    Seymour will step down on Dec. 31 and remain with the Fort Worth, Texas-based carrier in an advisory capacity through the first quarter of 2027, CEO Robert Isom announced Friday.

    According to recent reports, seymour has served as American’s chief operating officer since 2020. He joined the airline in 1999 and held various leadership positions overseeing technical operations, crew scheduling, and flight operations.

    “He’s the guy you want in the room when the stakes are high,” Isom wrote in a letter to employees.

    Industry observers note that jonCarlo “JC” Gulbranson, American’s current senior vice president of operations, will succeed Seymour on Jan. 1. He will report directly to Isom and assume oversight of the carrier’s technical operations, safety, and regulatory compliance teams.

    Gulbranson began his airline career at Northwest Airlines in 2000 before joining US Airways in 2008. He helped oversee the integration of flight operations systems following the merger with American.

    American will also move its corporate security team under its government affairs division. A latest reporting structure for the airline’s regional operations will be announced in December.

    “For nearly three decades, jet fuel hasn’t just been in my veins. It’s been part of my DNA. To this day, I wake up excited to get to work — which is just about all you can ask for in a job,” Seymour wrote in a LinkedIn post.

    The changes follow a broader management reshuffle declared in August as the carrier works to narrow its profitability gap with competitors Delta and United.

    #19435. Why Delta Air Lines' Brand-New Airbus A321neos Sat In The Desert While Flying 44 Recliners Instead

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1845 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Why Delta Air Lines' Brand-New Airbus A321neos Sat In The Desert While Flying 44 Recliners Instead

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1845 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that when airlines order a newly introduced fleet of aircraft, the assumption is usually straightforward - the aircraft arrive from the manufacturer, crews are trained, routes are assigned, and passengers begin flying on them shortly afterward.
    • Sources indicate that the story is not really about a dispute between an airline and a seat manufacturer.
    • Delta's A321neo premium transcontinental program was supposed to represent a major step forward in the airline's domestic premium offering.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that when airlines order a newly introduced fleet of aircraft, the assumption is usually straightforward - the aircraft arrive from the manufacturer, crews are trained, routes are assigned, and passengers begin flying on them shortly afterward. Yet Delta Air Lines' newest Airbus A321neos have become an unusual example of how a single component can disrupt an entire fleet strategy. Rather than entering service with the premium cabins they were designed to showcase, several of the airline's newest narrowbody aircraft spent months sitting in desert storage while the carrier searched for a way to make them operational.

    Sources indicate that the story is not really about a dispute between an airline and a seat manufacturer. Instead, it is a case study in how modern airline products have become so specialized that a single certification delay can ripple through fleet planning, network strategy, customer experience, and competitive positioning. In the case of Delta, the matter became so severe that the airline ultimately introduced a temporary cabin featuring 44 domestic first class recliner seats on aircraft originally intended to offer one of the most advanced premium transcontinental products in the US.

    Delta's A321neo premium transcontinental program was supposed to represent a major step forward in the airline's domestic premium offering. The aircraft were expected to operate some of the carrier's most crucial routes, particularly those linking major coastal business markets where travelers increasingly expect an experience that rivals international business class, such as Upcoming York John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) and Los Angeles International Airport (LAX).

    Industry observers note that at the center of the strategy was the Safran Vue business class seat. Unlike traditional herringbone layouts that angle passengers toward the aisle, the Vue featured a reverse-herringbone design that positioned passengers toward the window. The concept promised privacy, comfort, and views, giving the SkyTeam carrier a product that looked noticeably different from what competitors were offering.

    Sources indicate that the planned cabin reflected that premium focus, with each aircraft featuring 16 lie-flat business class suites, 12 premium economy seats, 54 Comfort+ seats, and 66 economy class seats. The layout balanced high-yield premium demand with the practical need to carry a substantial number of leisure travelers.

    That strategy was hardly surprising, given that premium transcontinental travel has become one of the most competitive segments of the US airline industry. Travelers flying between markets such as Latest York, Los Angeles, San Francisco, Boston, and Seattle increasingly expect direct aisle access, lie-flat seating, upgraded dining, and enhanced privacy. Airlines have responded by investing heavily in premium cabins, often treating them as key differentiators. For Delta, the Safran Vue was more than just another seat. It was intended to become a signature product that would reinforce the airline's premium positioning while helping it stand out from products such as JetBlue Airways' Mint and American Airlines' Flagship Suite.

    Reports emerging throughout 2025 and 2026 pointed toward persistent certification challenges involving the Safran Vue seat. While passengers often focus on comfort, privacy, and aesthetics, every airline seat must also satisfy extensive safety requirements before regulators allow it to enter commercial service.

    The reported challenges centered on certification standards set by the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), including human factors testing and crashworthiness requirements. These standards are designed to ensure that passengers can evacuate safely, move through the cabin efficiently, and remain protected during emergency situations. Even seemingly small changes to a seat's geometry can trigger extensive review processes.

    Industry observers have suggested that the difficulties expose a broader challenge facing the airline interiors sector, and over the past decade, premium airline seats have become increasingly complex. Features such as privacy doors, large entertainment screens, charging systems, storage compartments, and customized shell designs have transformed business class seats into highly sophisticated products, while regulators remain focused on ensuring safety standards are maintained regardless of how innovative a design may be. That can create tension between manufacturers seeking differentiation and regulators seeking consistency.

    The Safran Vue was not simply another variation of an existing product - its reverse-herringbone layout represented a notable departure from more conventional designs. Every departure from established layouts can generate additional questions during certification, particularly when passenger movement and evacuation procedures are involved.

    Sources indicate that for Delta, the result was a growing disconnect between aircraft deliveries and cabin readiness. The airline's fleet strategy assumed the premium product would be available when the aircraft arrived, but instead, aircraft began arriving while the seat certification process remained unresolved.

    Perhaps the most remarkable aspect is that Delta had already accepted delivery of several A321neos during 2024. Under normal circumstances, taking delivery marks the start of an aircraft's operational life, and airlines spend billions on fleet renewal programs because they expect those assets to begin generating revenue as quickly as possible.

    Without certified seats, however, the aircraft could not enter service in the originally intended form. Delta therefore faced a difficult decision - it could continue waiting indefinitely for certification progress, or it could temporarily remove the aircraft from active planning until a solution emerged. The result was the unusual sight of factory-fresh Airbus A321neos sitting in desert storage, with such facilities more commonly associated with retired aircraft, seasonal fleet adjustments, or aircraft awaiting resale.

    The situation demonstrated how dependent modern airline programs can become on individual suppliers. Airbus had delivered the aircraft, pilots and flight attendants could be trained, and routes could be scheduled, yet a single unresolved component prevented the intended product from entering service. There were also significant financial implications. While airlines rarely pay published list prices, an Airbus A321neo still represents a major investment, and every month spent parked in storage reduced utilization and delayed revenue that those aircraft were expected to generate.

    Sources indicate that beyond the direct financial impact, the delays complicated broader fleet planning. Airlines carefully coordinate aircraft deliveries with staffing, maintenance schedules, route launches, and network growth initiatives. When newly delivered aircraft suddenly become unavailable, those plans often require adjustment, turning what was once a seat certification challenge into a broader operational issue.

    Faced with ongoing uncertainty, Delta eventually opted for a practical workaround. Rather than waiting indefinitely for the intended lie-flat business class suites, the airline developed a temporary cabin configuration that would allow the aircraft to begin carrying passengers. Introduced in May, the interim layout transformed the aircraft into something unlike any other narrowbody right now flying for the carrier. Instead of the planned mix of business class suites and premium economy seating, the aircraft received a large domestic first class cabin featuring 44 recliner seats.

    According to recent reports, the complete configuration consists of 44 first class seats, 54 Comfort+ seats, and 66 economy class seats. Compared with the original design, the temporary layout dramatically increases the number of premium seats while eliminating the lie-flat product that was supposed to define the aircraft. In effect, Delta created an aircraft that remains heavily weighted toward premium travelers while avoiding the certification complications associated with the original seats. From an operational standpoint, the decision makes sense, as aircraft create value when they are flying, not when they are parked in storage. By introducing a temporary configuration, Delta could finally deploy the aircraft across its network and begin generating revenue from them.

    In a recent development, the move also demonstrates the airline's desire to maintain momentum. Waiting years for certification problems to be resolved would have left valuable aircraft sitting idle, so while the interim product differs significantly from the original vision, it lets Delta use the fleet while longer-term decisions are made. At the same time, every flight operated with 44 recliners instead of lie-flat suites serves as a reminder of how different the final product may have been had the original strategy proceeded on schedule.

    Industry observers note that the temporary cabin solved one major challenge, but it also created several unusual operational quirks, including lavatory access within the enlarged first class cabin. With 44 premium passengers seated at the front of the aircraft and only a single forward lavatory, the passenger-to-bathroom ratio is unusually high for a premium-heavy cabin where convenience is typically emphasized.

    Industry observers note that on longer Transcontinental routes, the arrangement could create queues that passengers would not normally associate with a premium experience. One traditional advantage of premium cabins is reduced competition for onboard facilities. The temporary layout partially undermines that benefit simply because of the unusually large number of first class seats.

    According to recent reports, the customer experience also differs considerably from what Delta originally intended. The carrier's domestic first class recliner seats remain comfortable, particularly on shorter flights, but they fall into a different category than private lie-flat suites. Travelers expecting a cutting-edge premium cabin may instead get a more traditional domestic experience.

    Recent findings suggest that crew operations are also affected, as boarding procedures, meal service, and passenger interactions all change when 44 passengers occupy the premium cabin. While none of these challenges are insurmountable, they create a unique operating environment compared with the airline's original looks, and in many ways, the lavatory issue has become symbolic of the broader situation - it highlights how an airline can end up making unexpected compromises when a key component of its long-term strategy fails to arrive on schedule.

    According to recent reports, the biggest question now concerns the program's future. Reports suggest Delta may be considering abandoning the Safran Vue altogether and adopting the Thompson Vantage Solo seat instead. Such a move would represent more than a simple supplier change. The Thompson Vantage Solo is already used by airlines, including JetBlue and American Airlines, and follows a more conventional aisle-facing herringbone layout; while potentially easier to certify, it would eliminate one of the key differentiators that Delta originally hoped to bring to market.

    From a practical perspective, switching to a proven product could reduce uncertainty and accelerate deployment. Airlines generally prefer predictable solutions when schedules, fleet looks, and customer expectations are involved, and a seat with an established certification history may appear increasingly attractive after years of delays. There would also be strategic consequences, as the window-facing reverse-herringbone concept was intended to provide a unique selling point. Replacing it with a more conventional product would therefore narrow the distinction between Delta and its competitors in the premium transcontinental market.

    Meanwhile, competitors continue investing in their own premium products. JetBlue Mint remains a strong force in premium transcontinental markets, while American Airlines continues rolling out newer Flagship Suite concepts. Against that backdrop, delays to the Airbus A321neo premium program also influence how Delta positions itself within one of the industry's most competitive markets.

    Whether Delta ultimately waits for the Safran Vue, adopts the Thompson Vantage Solo, or pursues another alternative entirely, the episode has already become a fascinating example of how modern airline strategies can hinge on remarkably specific details. A single seat design intended to create a competitive advantage instead delayed a flagship product, sent brand-new aircraft into desert storage, and forced Delta to fly one of the most unusual premium cabin configurations right now operating in the US.

    #19434. American officially retires its most exclusive long-haul seat: Bittersweet or overdue?

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (795 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thepointsguy ↗ Open Full Page

    American officially retires its most exclusive long-haul seat: Bittersweet or overdue?

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (795 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thepointsguy

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This week, the carrier (officially) bid farewell to Flagship First international service.
    • We’ve been talking for years about American’s looks to retire its international-style first-class product.
    • The airline is replacing Flagship First with larger and more modern business-class cabins on its marquee planes — cabins that will feature its next-generation Flagship Suites.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It’s the end of an era at American Airlines.

    This week, the carrier (officially) bid farewell to Flagship First international service.

    We’ve been talking for years about American’s looks to retire its international-style first-class product.

    The airline is replacing Flagship First with larger and more modern business-class cabins on its marquee planes — cabins that will feature its next-generation Flagship Suites.

    For a lot of flyers, that’s likely to be a positive shift: It will mean a host of upgrades in business-class, including seats with sliding privacy doors and superior tech.

    But there’s at least a little nostalgia in bidding farewell to a cabin that, for many years, was billed as American’s most exclusive.

    Sources indicate that american was the last U.S. airline that claimed to offer a standalone, international first-class product.

    Across the global airline industry, many carriers sunset long-haul first-class years ago, choosing to instead offer more — and improved — business-class seats, which take up less space and are considered more profitable.

    For years, Delta Air Lines’ Delta One business-class suites have been its premier long-haul offering.

    United Airlines bid farewell to international first class in 2018 when it pivoted to Polaris business class.

    That left American’s Flagship First as a relic, of sorts, in the U.S. airline industry — and even on its own planes.

    In recent years, you could only find the cabin on two fleet types American operated: its Boeing 777-300ER, which offered eight of the pods up front in their own dedicated cabin.

    Plus, AA still (for now) offers Flagship First on its three-cabin Airbus A321T, which has been a fixture on lucrative coast-to-coast routes like Upcoming York to Los Angeles and San Francisco.

    But soon, it will be a thing of the past on both planes.

    American is retrofitting its larger 777s, ditching first-class in favor of 70 all-new Flagship Suites in business-class — along with the biggest premium economy cabin it’s ever offered.

    Related: This is now American Airlines' most premium plane: Here's what it's like on board.

    On domestic routes, the A321T will actually keep flying with Flagship First through March 28.

    But after that, AA will stop selling the Flagship First cabin on the A321T configuration, which is eventually going away as American flexes in its new A321XLR planes fully onto its top cross-country flights.

    In a lot of ways, American ditching Flagship First is a positive (and arguably overdue) transition for flyers.

    It’ll give passengers more lie-flat seats to pick from, whether they’re paying cash, using AAdvantage miles or using a systemwide upgrade.

    Also — while those Flagship First seats were really spacious and comfortable, many would say that American's new business-class product is a major upgrade from what it previously offered in that cabin.

    On some planes, that even includes extra-spacious Flagship Suites Preferred in the front and bulkhead rows of some planes, which offer a lot more space.

    Value check: Is it worth buying up to American Airlines' new business-class Flagship Suite Preferred?

    Beyond the aircraft, American also intends to still offer many of the same amenities for business-class that first-class passengers historically enjoyed.

    Sources indicate that for instance, its Flagship business-class tickets get access to its premium lounges. Passengers traveling in Flagship Business and Flagship Business Plus on qualifying international, transcontinental and Hawaii routes will also be able to have a meal in its exclusive restaurant-style dining rooms in Dallas, Los Angeles and Miami.

    The experience is available on a space-available basis.

    So, in some ways, you could argue the end of Flagship First is more symbolic than anything.

    But for some AA loyalists, it's still a little bittersweet.

    TPG’s Clint Henderson is our resident Flagship First enthusiast, having flown the cabin on dozens of occasions.

    "The service in first class wasn't particularly differentiated, but I still liked a few of the special touches," he stated, pointing to the additional soup course and appetizer, along with a handful of elevated amenities.

    He especially appreciated the “La-Z-Boy-style” seats at the front of American’s 777s, which could lie flat or swivel and turn into an “office in the sky.”.

    “While these cabins are definitely showing their age,” Henderson added, “I’m sad to see it go.”.

    While Flagship First is technically going away as an official cabin on international service, the seats themselves won't disappear overnight.

    According to recent reports, so far, American has only retrofitted one of its 20 Boeing 777-300ERs that feature the seats. That means a handful of jets with the old first-class seats will still be flying around well into 2027.

    According to recent reports, going forward, the former Flagship First seats on those planes will be marketed as business-class. They won’t come with the full first-class service, but you’ll still get the elevated seat.

    White House budget aide Ueland slated to head GAO

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1108 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 2 official at the White House Office of Management and Budget, arrives for his confirmation hearing in the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on April 3, 2025.
    • President Donald Trump on Monday nominated Eric Ueland, deputy director for management in the White House budget office, to be the next comptroller general to lead the Government Accountability Office.
    • The nomination fills in the blanks after Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., had scheduled a Nov.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Eric Ueland, No. 2 official at the White House Office of Management and Budget, arrives for his confirmation hearing in the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on April 3, 2025. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    President Donald Trump on Monday nominated Eric Ueland, deputy director for management in the White House budget office, to be the next comptroller general to lead the Government Accountability Office.

    The nomination fills in the blanks after Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., had scheduled a Nov. 19 hearing to examine more than a dozen of Trump’s nominees for executive and judicial positions but without identifying who the comptroller general candidate would be. Ueland's name has since been added to the hearing agenda.

    The move sets up an unprecedented scenario where a top official of the Office of Management and Budget, a White House office that has tangled with the Government Accountability Office since Trump’s first term, is put forward as the next head of the legislative agency.

    The GAO, a congressional watchdog with some 3,000 employees, has repeatedly accused the administration of violating the 1974 budget law by withholding or "impounding" enacted, appropriated funds. In September, for example, the GAO said Trump’s cancellation of $810 million in spending without the approval of Congress through a so-called pocket rescission was illegal.

    White House Budget Director Russ Vought was quick to respond on X, writing that GAO “has become hyper partisan and ... they make their legal assessments based on whether Democrats are in the White House.” The administration has dismissed GAO opinions, arguing the agency has no authority over the executive branch because it is part of the legislative branch.

    Democrats immediately denounced Ueland's nomination, saying it promised to further inflame tensions between the executive and legislative branches over the power of the purse.

    “It would be lunacy for the Senate to hand a 15-year term leading Congress’ nonpartisan watchdog to a Russ Vought acolyte who spends his days plotting new ways for this administration to defy Congress," said Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash., who is likely to chair the panel next year.

    "Ueland orchestrated the president’s destructive mass firing campaign, is presiding over the razing of USAID, and is the last person who should be leading GAO," Murray said in a statement.

    In a recent development, sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich., ranking member of the Homeland Security committee, urged all senators to oppose the Ueland nomination, saying it would provide “further power to the Executive Branch at a time when independent oversight from Congress is needed more than ever.”.

    Peters also reiterated his previous criticism of Republicans for skipping bipartisan deliberations by a special 10-member legislative commission that is charged under statute with recommending candidates to the president for nomination.

    “All three times the Commission process has occurred in the past, the president has selected a nominee with bipartisan support,” Peters stated.

    In a sign of potential trouble for the nomination, a few Republicans expressed qualms about Ueland and what critics described as a rushed process for picking a GAO chief.

    "I'm not a fan," mentioned retiring Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., who faulted Ueland's boss for not providing proof of the cost savings claimed by Trump's Department of Government Efficiency, known as DOGE.

    According to recent reports, "To me, there's a lack of discipline or business experience in there to answer that simple question, or the reason they don't answer it is they don't have an answer," Tillis said. "Both are bad.".

    While Tillis stopped short of promising to oppose Ueland, he remarked the nomination "deserves individual consideration" instead of being taken up in a group with several other nominees.

    According to recent reports, and Sen. John Curtis, R-Utah, "has concerns that the nomination is too partisan, particularly given how independent and long-term the appointment of the Comptroller General is," a spokesman mentioned in a statement.

    Ueland has served as deputy director for management at the White House budget office since last year following his confirmation by the Senate on a party line 52-45 vote. He also has been performing the duties of the OMB controller since September 2025, according to his LinkedIn profile.

    An expert on legislative procedure and strategy, Ueland has worked in a wide range of administrative and policy-oriented positions in the executive branch — including at OMB, the State Department and White House — and before that in the Senate.

    He served as director of legislative affairs for Trump in his first term, as well as the State Department undersecretary for civilian security, democracy and human rights, and director of the department’s Office of U.S. Foreign Assistance, among other positions.

    It has been revealed that before that, he was the Senate Budget Committee’s GOP staff director under then-Chairman Michael B. Enzi, R-Wyo., for four years through the end of 2017.

    Earlier, he worked as chief of staff to then-Senate GOP Whip Don Nickles of Oklahoma and then-Senate Majority Leader Bill Frist of Tennessee.

    Ueland, who has a bachelor’s degree in history from the University of San Francisco, lacks the financial background of recent past comptrollers. He has, however, gone deep in the weeds with numbers at OMB and the Senate Budget Committee, and has extensive experience as an administrator.

    Sources indicate that former comptroller Charles A. Bowsher was a CPA, a partner at Arthur Anderson and assistant secretary of the Navy for financial management before President Ronald Reagan tapped him to lead the GAO in 1981.

    According to recent reports, david M. Walker, his successor, was a CPA, a partner at Arthur Anderson, assistant secretary of labor in the Employee Benefits Security Administration, and deputy executive director of the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation before his nomination by President Bill Clinton.

    Recent findings suggest that gene L. Dodaro, whose 15-year term ended last year, had a bachelor’s degree in accounting and had worked at GAO for some 35 years before President Barack Obama nominated him to succeed Walker.

    When Dodaro left, he designated Orice Williams Brown, who was GAO’s chief operating officer, as acting comptroller.

    In a recent development, before Trump nominated Ueland, the six Republican members of the legislative commission sent a letter to the White House last week recommending three candidates for the position — Ueland, Brian C. DeBusk and Roland Foster, according to sources.

    Industry observers note that deBusk is president and CEO of DeRoyal Industries, a privately held medical equipment manufacturer. He served on the Medicare Payment Advisory Commission from 2016 to 2022 after being appointed by Dodaro. Foster is a longtime GOP aide currently serving as senior adviser to retiring Sen. Joni Ernst, R-Iowa.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that aeromexico is planning some major upgrades to its wide body fleet, which consists exclusively of Boeing 787s. This is interesting on many levels — we’ll see the larger Dreamliners get all-new business class cabins plus premium economy for the first time, we’ll see the smaller Dreamliners get the old business class cabins of the bigger Dreamliners, and we’ll see the airline adopt some Delta-style branding.

    To start, let me provide the context that Aeromexico’s Boeing 787 fleet currently consists of 25 planes, including:.

    Aeromexico is planning on fully overhauling the premium cabins on these planes, as was announced by the company’s CEO at this week’s APEX FTE EXPO 2026.

    The plan is for the 787-9s to get all-newly introduced cabins, and in the process, the 787-8s will get the old business class seats from the 787-9s. That means the 787-8s will get reverse herringbone seats, which are still competitive, but of course not cutting edge (though still a huge improvement over the pairs of seats right now on the planes).

    The 787-9s will really become the next-generation flagship planes for the airline, though some patience will be required. The expectation is that the first of these Dreamliners will be retrofitted in the next 18 to 24 months (so hopefully by some point in 2028), and then it’ll likely take a couple of years for the fleet to be upgraded.

    It has been revealed that we’ll talk more about the upcoming business class product as such in a bit, but the idea is that the 787-9s will get business class suites, including a front row “business class plus” product. On top of that, the 787-9s will be getting a premium economy cabin for the first time.

    In a recent development, the plane will also have up to 70% more premium seats than before. At the moment, Aeromexico’s 787-9s have 36 business class seats, while the retrofitted planes will have a total of 61 premium seats, between business class and premium economy. So I suspect the business class cabin won’t actually get that much bigger, but instead, most of that premium addition will come in the form of the new premium economy cabin.

    It’s also worth mentioning that Aeromexico is adopting some Delta-style branding, as Delta owns a 20% stake in Aeromexico, and the two airlines have a close partnership.

    Aeromexico’s upcoming premium products will be known as Premier One Suites Plus (the “business class plus” product), Premier One Suites (business class), and Premier (premium economy). It seems the 787-8 business class will just be branded as Premier One, given the lack of suites with doors. That all sure seems to be inspired by the Delta One branding that’s used by the carrier’s partner.

    Seth Miller from PaxEx.Aero flags how Aeromexico’s upcoming Boeing 787-9 business class suite is from Recaro, as the airline is reportedly the launch customer for this new product. However, the exact product hasn’t actually been named.

    According to recent reports, aeromexico CEO Dr. Andres Conesa unveiled the carrier's fresh premium economy cabin plus refreshed business class seat at #APEXFTEExpo in Singapore this week.Full teaser video in the story: paxex.aero/first-look-a….#PaxEx$RTX.

    I believe this might be an evolution of the Recaro R7 product (LATAM’s newest 787 business class), which in and of itself was already an evolution of the Recaro CL6720 product (Iberia’s newest A350 business class).

    It seems that what was unveiled earlier this year was the upcoming Recaro R7 Horizon concept, which is the same idea, but with upgraded technology and customization.

    I imagine that we’ll learn more in the coming months, as this was an unusual way to unveil a fresh product. But this does seem to be officially happening, so it’s something to look forward to… down the road.

    Industry observers note that aeromexico is planning some substantial upgrades to its Dreamliners. The Boeing 787-9s will be getting all-fresh cabins, including new business class suites, plus a premium economy cabin for the first time. There will even be a premium business product in the first row, with the products marketed as Premier One Suites Plus, Premier One Suites, and Premier.

    In a recent development, as this happens, the 787-8s will be getting the old reverse herringbone seats from the 787-9s, so that will be a meaningful upgrade as well. You can expect these new cabins to roll out starting at some point in 2028, so some patience will be required. I can’t wait to learn more!

    A upcoming deal with Miami-Dade County will help American Airlines solidify and eventually expand its maintenance operations at Miami International Airport.

    Sources indicate that the county announced this week that it will buy a hangar and maintenance space at Miami International from a third-party owner and lease it directly to American for its MRO operations. The acquisition includes Hangar 890, Building 891, 10.2 acres of land, and a 2.2-acre parking lot.

    According to recent reports, according to the Miami Herald, American already leases the property and uses it for maintenance work, but a change in ownership from private jet operator Aero Miami to the county will give American more leeway to develop the space as it sees fit. The new lease with the county will run for 20 years and cost American $67.8 million, the newspaper mentioned.

    In a recent development, the airline plans to keep more than 650 aircraft maintenance workers at the facility. It has also agreed to complete about $13.9 million in building repairs.

    Industry observers note that “Miami is a cornerstone of American’s international network and a consequential part of our long-term growth strategy,” American Senior Vice President of Miami Operations Juan Carlos Liscano said in a news release. “This agreement reinforces our dedication to our Miami team and preserves our ability to continue growing our network to more destinations around the world for our customers.”.

    American is the largest airline at Miami, carrying more than half of all passengers there.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Emirates is known for its incredibly high service standards, and that’s largely thanks to the hierarchical system onboard. You have different ranks of flight attendants, then you have supervisors overseeing business class and economy, and then those supervisors report to the purser.

    This system ensures that there’s accountability onboard, and I think that lack of hierarchy is one of the reasons we have service concerns at airlines in the US, as no one is really in charge. Anyway, along those lines, Emirates has just introduced a new initiative, which will no doubt be controversial among flight attendants….

    Emirates has a rank above pursers, which are the Standard Pursers (which is a weird name, but the idea is that they’re there to audit and enforce “standards”). These are specially trained former pursers who no longer work flights in a standard capacity (at least until now), but instead, they audit the crews onboard flights. They have completely different uniforms.

    Emirates’ Chief Operations Officer, Adel Alredha, has just taken to Instagram to highlight a new initiative involving this small group of employees:.

    On 3 November, Emirates introduced a new initiative on select flights, which will have Standard Pursers work alongside cabin crew teams to provide support and guidance to ensure consistently high standards of service.

    This step reflects the airline’s ongoing commitment to maintaining service quality and elevating the customer experience.

    So rather than just auditing the cabins, these Emirates employees will actually be working in the cabin, and that’s sure to ruffle some feathers….

    A post shared by Adel Alredha (@adelalredha).

    Emirates is of course an incredibly global airline with staff from around the world, and I know a thing or two about the internal politics that crews deal with, the different working environments based on who is purser, etc.

    For example, you have some pursers who are incredibly strict to the point that they make their colleagues feel uncomfortable and nervous, while you have other pursers who try to encourage good service by creating a fun environment, etc.

    It goes without saying that historically when a flight had an auditor onboard, everyone would be on their absolute best behavior. In a way that’s no doubt a bit chaotic and stressful, since they’re worried about repercussions if something goes wrong.

    According to recent reports, when it comes to this initiative, on the one hand, it’s probably good for these auditors to get some renewed firsthand experience with service, guest expectations, etc. On the other hand, I have to imagine that from the perspective of other crew members, this won’t necessarily be perceived as an effort to “provide support and guidance.”.

    As one commenter on the Instagram post notes, “this is like sending a child to school along with mama with a stick to correct the kid every step.” Another commenter notes “as if there wasn’t already enough pressure on the crew.”.

    Sources indicate that I am curious if these flights are still staffed with a regular purser in addition to this special rank of purser, because that could also cause a bit of a butting-of-heads. If an auditor is onboard in their official capacity, it’s clear what everyone’s role onboard is (everyone is there to make sure they perform well!). But if the auditor is there to simply “provide support,” that blurs the lines a little bit, no?

    Recent findings suggest that anyway, there aren’t actually that many of these auditor pursers at the airline, so presumably only a small percentage of flights will have them. But if you do notice a crew member with a completely different uniform (more silver in color), now you know what’s going on. That would also be a great person to provide any feedback to, because they actually have the ability to get those details to the right person.

    Emirates has Standard Pursers, who are essentially auditors who are assigned select flights, in order to evaluate service from the crew. As of this month, these auditors are also starting to work on flights alongside the crew, to “provide support and guidance.”.

    Recent findings suggest that there’s no denying that this is an initiative that will make some crew members nervous, since this definitely blurs the line of auditing vs. having an extra set of helping hands. However, given the relatively small number of auditors, they shouldn’t be on too many flights. But if you do see someone in a completely different uniform (other than the standard female purser uniform), then now you know what’s going on.

    What do you make of this Emirates initiative?

    In a recent development, why would an auditor on board create stress? If you are doing what you are supposed to be doing, then there would not be a problem. That auditor that write up how wonderfully well you performed your duties and are ready for promotion.

    I am a predominantly ground based cabin crew manager for a large European airline but also work as supernumerary crew on 2-3 long haul flights per year. On those flights I wear a uniform and am additional to the crew complement and my role is to support and to a lesser degree assess member of my flying team. I find it really beneficial as airline crew are typically remote workers and rarely have access to their ground manager. It also gives me the ability to see first hand lots of the pain points my team complain to me about - service routines, galley layouts etc. I don't think these kind of roles are that unusual in the airline world. We just aren't called 'Standard Pursers' ouch.

    If they're not "working" the flight, I could perceive this not going well with customers as well in a way: if you see people constantly passing by you and never checking on you, or if you ask that person for help and they direct it to another person, then it could come across the wrong way. Imagine you press the call attendant button and the Standard Purser just walks right by you. You'd probably think that you're being ignored by staff / they're slacking off.

    If only all airlines had in-flight service auditors, the skies would be a better place.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that in the past week, American Airlines revealed more changes to its huge network. They all involve Los Angeles International Airport, at which the oneworld member is the third-largest operator for passengers, flights, seats for sale, and available seat miles.

    Recent findings suggest that american's schedule submission to OAG highlights that Los Angeles is the carrier's ninth-busiest hub for departures this year. It rises to eighth for available seats and seventh for ASMs. And for passenger traffic, which is obviously retrospective, it was eighth through August. While Los Angeles is not a huge hub for American, the route changes are notable.

    In the latest schedule upgrade, two of the following three routes will now be removed in early 2027. The plan was for them to be served daily through 2027, although Cleveland was to have only a handful of services in April and May before being ramped up to daily again for the peak summer.

    Load Factor (Latest Data August 2026).

    Other Carriers From Los Angeles International In 2027?

    2013-2020 (two daily; mainly SkyWest CRJ200/CRJ700).

    According to recent reports, yes: Alaska Airlines (two daily E175 by Horizon Air and SkyWest). Also, Alaska Airlines runs from Burbank and Allegiant from Orange County. Allegant previously served the city from Los Angeles.

    2026 only (mainly daily; 737-800, 737 MAX 8).

    Yes: United (two daily 737 MAX 8, MAX 9). No flights from other airports in the LA Basin.

    75.5% (October 2025-August 2026 only).

    According to recent reports, no. It is now unserved. However, Allegiant operates between Orange County and Des Moines, having previously flown from Los Angeles.

    The link to Eugene, Oregon, is notable. This route last had regular flights with American — or, strictly speaking, SkyWest operating for American Eagle on behalf of American — six years ago. AeroRoutes reveals that the northbound market was due to return in 2027, but now it won't. American's network to Eugene has halved, with only Phoenix still served.

    The carrier removed various other routes from Los Angeles in 2025 or 2026, but they don't really count as they weren't 'normal' operations. They included the intra-Californian links to San José (for the Super Bowl) and Palm Springs (for Coachella), along with the transborder Toronto (for the Toronto International Film Festival). Some may return in 2027. The main exception was Flagstaff, which had a weekly service through May 2025.

    Focusing on December 2026 through next summer, all the following links are due to see American or its regional unit. As is usually the case with the US Massive Three carriers, all have previously been served, albeit not necessarily always regularly.

    For example, having previously been served for years, the last regular operations to Reno were five years ago. However, the route has had irregular flights each year, most recently in September 2026, seemingly for the Burning Man festival. Regular flights are coming back.

    Head-To-Head Competition From Los Angeles International In 2027?

    Industry observers note that yes: Delta (up to daily SkyWest E175, but only weekly when American will operate) and United (up to two daily; 737 MAX 8 and SkyWest E175). No flights from other airports in the city.

    It has been revealed that yes: in 2017 and again in 2021. Third time a charm?

    In a recent development, no. American will be the only operator from the LA Basin. Los Angeles-Grand Junction was served by Allegiant until 2024.

    3 daily SkyWest CRJ700 and E175.

    Yes: 1999 to 2003, with regular flights from 2010 until 2021. Third time lucky?

    Yes: Delta (four daily SkyWest E175), Southwest (daily 737-700, 737 MAX 8), United (up to three daily 737-800, SkyWest E175). Southwest also runs from Burbank and Long Beach.

    Excluding the now-ending service to Cleveland, which began in April 2026, American has only inaugurated one other route from Los Angeles this year. It was to Washington Dulles, which was previously on the carrier's map for many years until 2020.

    American returned to Dulles in April 2026 and runs daily on the 737 MAX 8, although the A321ceo and A321neo will appear briefly in 2027. Two daily flights existed until early 2020 while three were last available in 2017.

    Recent findings suggest that let's look at March to October 2027, after the routes that are ending will have been removed. American plans an average of 143 daily departures, up from 133 daily in the same period in 2026. As of November 20 and subject to change, 56 routes will be available, which includes the time-limited operation to Louisville for the Kentucky Derby.

    With 143 daily departures, American will have a fifth of all services from Los Angeles International. While activity has jumped by 7% in a year, which is very strong in itself, it is the slowest expansion of the top three operators. Delta is up by 16% while United has added 10% more services.

    • Senate Republicans appeared skeptical Monday about the need for as much as $50 billion to upgrade the nation’s aging air traffic control system, after a nationwide ground stop last Friday prompted the massive, increased asking price from top administration officials.
    • Speaking with reporters, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., noted he believed the department still had about $8 billion outstanding from an air traffic control modernization package included in last year’s reconciliation law.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., speaks with reporters on Nov. 10. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Senate Republicans appeared skeptical Monday about the need for as much as $50 billion to upgrade the nation’s aging air traffic control system, after a nationwide ground stop last Friday prompted the massive, increased asking price from top administration officials.

    Speaking with reporters, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., noted he believed the department still had about $8 billion outstanding from an air traffic control modernization package included in last year’s reconciliation law.

    “I got to obviously see the explanation behind it, or sort of laying out the numbers why it's necessary,” Thune noted of the $50 billion, which jumped from $30 billion a day earlier.

    Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told reporters he was unimpressed by Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s request and that he wanted to see a breakdown of how the department would use the funds.

    “They got to give us an upgrade,” Tillis remarked. “I mean, the $50 billion request — I thought that was $30 billion. So people have got to explain to me, really, even the basis for the $30 billion, let alone the additional $20 billion that Duffy mentioned the other day.”.

    Sen. John Hoeven, R-N.D., similarly said legislators would need “more detail” on the request but said “obviously there needs to be more” funding for the modernization efforts.

    Hoeven serves on the Senate Transportation-HUD Appropriations Subcommittee, which rolled out a fiscal 2027 spending bill Monday that would increase the FAA’s annual allocation to facilities and equipment by $500 million, a nearly 13 percent boost.

    Duffy is slotted to attend the Senate GOP conference lunch on Tuesday, where he is likely to be peppered with such requests for specifics. Meanwhile, FAA staff are expected to brief House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee aides on Tuesday, after that meeting got pushed on Monday.

    The Senate’s go-slow approach is in contrast to Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., who stated over the weekend that he would add the $50 billion request to a year-end legislative package.

    Sources indicate that the White House’s call for additional funds ballooned last week in the aftermath of the nationwide ground stop that created confusion and concern at airports around the country. The Federal Aviation Administration remarked Sunday that the unusual move was made “out of an abundance of caution” after legacy equipment became flooded with data during routine upgrades.

    The FAA’s initial investigation tied the data flooding to work being done at a radar site in Texas and a radio communications site in Arkansas by contractor L3Harris Technologies.

    Speaking on CNBC’s Squawk Box, Duffy remarked the server thought to have caused the flooding was taken to the L3Harris lab in Florida where FAA personnel are working with the FBI to analyze the router that likely caused the system instability.

    Still, as administration officials attempt to understand the system errors that led to the ground stop, Duffy has used the moment as justification to lobby for additional funds.

    “In this old telecom network, I do have money to switch over from the old copper wires to fiber and we’re 70 percent completed with that mission, but we need a brand upcoming architecture for our telecom and aviation,” Duffy stated on CNBC Monday. “This can happen rapidly to build a new state of the art telecom network, it’s just that it has to be funded.”.

    According to recent reports, A day before the incident, Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought wrote to congressional appropriators, formally asking for $30.1 billion in added funds for the modernization effort, in line with a bill introduced by Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., in late September. That ask inexplicably jumped up to $50 billion by Friday night in the aftermath of the ground stop.

    On Monday, Thune noted the prior request for approximately $30 billion, which he remarked included “some other stuff” as well.

    Schmitt’s bill and the White House request would provide $10.1 billion for air traffic control upgrades, including $7.2 billion for a “common automation platform and a common controller workstation,” and $2 billion for cloud computing and telecommunications infrastructure.

    Another $10 billion would go toward airport improvement projects, including $2 billion to “construct, replace, and improve terminal air traffic control facilities, including activities using digital tower technologies.”.

    The request includes $10 billion for a terminal modernization or reconstruction pilot program for certain midsized airports.

    Thune mentioned Monday that he tallied about $12 billion in the upcoming request specifically for air traffic control related complications, likely a reference to the $10.1 billion plus the $2 billion for terminal facilities.

    “I think there's more we need to figure out, and obviously I think we all agree that we need to be modernizing and updating, particularly in an area like that where safety is the number one priority, but also we want to do that in a smart way and make sure that we're using taxpayer dollars wisely and well,” Thune said. “We’ll hear him out.”.

    Meanwhile, Democrats kept up the drumbeat of criticism, both for the airspace management that led to the ground stop and the rollout of the new funding request.

    “So typical of this incompetent administration — they have money, they don’t use it and then they come back and say ‘give us more money,'” Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., noted on the floor.

    Savannah Behrmann and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

    Bilt is the platform known for providing rewards for housing payments. Earlier this year we saw massive changes at Bilt, including an overhaul of the credit card portfolio, plus latest ways that housing rewards are offered.

    There are many innovative things about Bilt, including that there’s a Bilt Rent Day promotion on the first day of each month.     There are a couple of aspects to the Bilt Rent Day promotion, including the ability to earn bonus points (which is the same every month), plus at least one additional promotion.

Personally, I think the Bilt Palladium Card is by far the most lucrative.

    It has been revealed that on the first day of each month, you earn double those rewards on these cards, and earn up to 1,000 bonus points each month. It could be worth strategically making some purchases on the first day of each month to maximize this as much as possible.

    For example, with double points, the Bilt Palladium Card offers 4x points on everyday spending on the first day of the month, so that’s pretty awesome (up to a cap of $500 worth of spending, since that would earn you 1,000 bonus points).

    On December 1, 2026, Bilt is offering a bonus when members redeem points for statement credits. The bonus you’re eligible for depends on which Bilt credit card you have, as follows:.

    On December 1, 2026, Bilt is offering a JetBlue TrueBlue Mosaic status match challenge, and the status you’re eligible for depends on your Bilt elite status, as follows:.

    It has been revealed that the status is matched for a period of three months, with no additional activity required to maintain it for that period. Then, during those three months, members can extend the status through January 31, 2028, by completing the following requirements:.

As a reminder, you earn one tile for every $100 spent on JetBlue, or every $1,000 spent on a co-branded JetBlue credit card. So renewing status requires anywhere from $1,000 to $4,000 of airfare spending, or $10,000 to $40,000 of credit card spending.

JetBlue is also offering a status match challenge, whereby Bilt members can receive Mosaic 1 or Mosaic 2 status for a period of 90 days, and can then extend status through early 2028, with the opportunity to earn up to Mosaic 3 status, based on how many tiles are earned.

    Why Aerolíneas Argentinas Is Basically An Ultra Low Cost Carrier In Disguise

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1864 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This might seem like a rather niche topic to cover in my first week at OMAAT, but after Ben mentioned this story in his intro article, I thought it made sense to follow up fast with an explainer.
    • As a flag carrier of the 3rd most populous nation in South America, I went into my Aerolíneas Argentinas flight with them at the start of the year expecting some pretty standard things: enjoying my SkyTeam benefits, lounge access, and, most importantly of all for someone living out of a suitcase, checked bag allowance.
    • However, I swiftly discovered that the airline is basically an ultra-low-cost airline masquerading as a full-service carrier.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This might seem like a rather niche topic to cover in my first week at OMAAT, but after Ben mentioned this story in his intro article, I thought it made sense to follow up fast with an explainer.

    As a flag carrier of the 3rd most populous nation in South America, I went into my Aerolíneas Argentinas flight with them at the start of the year expecting some pretty standard things: enjoying my SkyTeam benefits, lounge access, and, most importantly of all for someone living out of a suitcase, checked bag allowance.

    However, I swiftly discovered that the airline is basically an ultra-low-cost airline masquerading as a full-service carrier.

    Recent findings suggest that I needed to get from Buenos Aires to Mendoza for a friend’s 40th birthday celebrations. Options were pretty limited, with nonstop flights available with either JetSmart or, indeed, Aerolíneas Argentinas. I try to avoid low-cost airlines when possible, because, quite simply, I enjoy the flying experience, and low-cost airlines tend to suck every enjoyable element out of it.

    Other pros to booking Aerolíneas Argentinas, personally:.

    After researching my options, I used Flying Blue miles to book two single tickets from Buenos Aires Jorge Newbery Aeroparque Airport (AEP) to Mendoza’s El Plumerillo Airport (MDZ).

    I can’t remember how much the fares were when I was planning the trip, but each one-way flight cost a total of 7,500 miles and less than $10 in taxes and fees.

    Looking now at example fares for January next year, round-trips for Aerolíneas’ lowest and most restrictive fare category (more on that to come) start at around $120.

    In a recent development, I know it’s not a hard-and-fast rule, but I’ve come to expect that, most of the time, the baggage allowance listed on the booking confirmation is correct. This is often true with redemptions, such as British Airways, which notably offers and acknowledges a 23 kg baggage allowance when redeeming Avios, even for a short-haul flight in economy.

    The confirmation email I received clearly noted 1x checked bag with a 23 kg limit.

    Again, the attached PDF stated that I’d have 1x checked bag included.

    Industry observers note that as the Argentinian scamsters would have it, I learned at check-in that the airline has a 15 kg weight limit for checked bags on domestic flights. I tried to plead my case and showed the rather unhelpful check-in agent my booking confirmation, but he basically noted, “that means nothing.”.

    So they weigh your bag, give you a ticket, and then you have to exit the terminal building and find this little cashier where they collect their scammy little earnings. And what better place to proudly display a “SkyTeam Alliance Member” sign at the very desk where the airline also proudly collects baggage fees from SkyTeam elite status holders, even when traveling on award tickets?

    Once I’d been charged the fee of around $17, I had to join another queue back inside and show them I’d paid for the extra weight before they’d dispatch my bag. You might look at the $32 in fees I paid and think, “What is he complaining about?” But this isn’t about the actual amount of money; it’s the principle.

    Recent findings suggest that only after the debacle did I learn the extent of Aerolíneas Argentinas’ domestic fare restrictions. Imagine paying $510 (more than four times the cheapest fare) for a “premium economy” ticket and still only getting 15 kg checked baggage allowance, no Fast Pass, no priority boarding (what?), and no lounge access. The latter isn’t such a significant deal as Aerolíneas Argentinas doesn’t even have its own lounge at AEP.

    Airline loyalty is really key to me, and I generally value it more than the ability to redeem miles. Maybe I’ll get into that another day….

    Things got off to a fairly normal start when I saw the Sky Priority check-in kiosks at Aeroparque.

    Recent findings suggest that that feeling of normalcy lasted as long as it took me to get from the sign to the aforementioned conversation about the checked bag situation at the desk. Despite my very best efforts combining my Castilian Spanish and Geordie charm (we’re called Geordies where I’m from in the North East of England), the man at the check-in desk seemed to take real pleasure in explaining that the checked bag rules on my booking confirmation were irrelevant and I’d have to pay the fee.

    For what it’s worth, Sky Priority check-in was also available at Mendoza.

    Being nickel-and-dimed for a checked bag by a flag carrier airline is shameful.

    Back at Aeroparque, there was no fast track, and the security line was ridiculously long. That said, it’s rare in South America to have fast track lanes. For example, no matter whether you’re flying economy or first class (even Air France La Première), everyone waits in the same line to clear pre-departure passport control at São Paulo’s Guarulhos.

    Thanks to my Priority Pass, I did have access to the surprisingly nice AMAE lounge in the national departures part of the airport.

    In a recent development, even from the outside, my 15-year-old Embraer 190 looked like it had seen better days. The zebra-striped dirt streaks running from each window suggested this place hadn’t been washed or hit the maintenance hangar for a while.

    Inside the Embraer, however, could have been a lot worse. The older seats had thick padding, and despite being a small 2-2-configured cabin, it felt bright and spacious.

    It was the Uber advertising on every single headrest that I found most jarring.

    The legroom was decent, too. The retro seatback screens, on the other hand, were pretty much redundant.

    In a recent development, it was stepping on board the 16-year-old Boeing 737-700 back to Buenos Aires that Aerolíneas Argentinas’ low-costness was most glaring. Looking at this, I would never guess this plane belonged to a flag carrier. The seats were very uncomfortable, and I think I remember they didn’t recline either.

    As for service, I don’t recall it being particularly good or particularly bad. Forgettable is probably the most accurate word.

    Imagine the likes of Spirit (RIP) or Ryanair calling itself a national flag carrier; that’s basically what Aerolíneas Argentinas is. I’m planning a trip with my dad and brother for February next year that includes Argentina, and I will actively avoid flying Aerolíneas, even if it means forgoing the chance to earn any Flying Blue miles and XPs.

    Sources indicate that it’s almost as if the airline has been abandoned. After all, the only real competition is low-cost airlines at LATAM — the full-service carrier which dominates South America. Who knows, maybe things will change come 2028 when it takes delivery of fresh Airbus A330-900s and Boeing 737 MAXs.

    If I were a power that be at SkyTeam, I’d definitely remove the airline from the alliance. And if I had my way, Aerolíneas Argentinas would be bought by LATAM, and the cherry on top would be LATAM joining SkyTeam. I should probably put a business case together for that….

And any attempt to request compensation was lost in AR’s incredibly antiquated tech infrastructure. I eventually gave up. So my lesson learned was to not book a flight based on vibes.

    #19421. No more permanent coalitions: What the midterm results reveal

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (915 w)

    No more permanent coalitions: What the midterm results reveal

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (915 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 9 for a group photo with incoming members of his caucus: from left, Ohio's Sherrod Brown, Texas' James Talarico, Iowa's Josh Turek, Michigan's Abdul El-Sayed, North Carolina's Roy Cooper, Illinois' Juliana Stratton, New Hampshire's Chris Pappas, South Carolina's Annie Andrews, Minnesota's Peggy Flanagan, Maine's Troy Jackson and Kansas' Adam Hamilton.
    • It has been revealed that ANALYSIS -- “Life moves pretty fast,” that famed 20th-century philosopher Ferris Bueller once mentioned.
    • Recent findings suggest that in 2024, Democrats were consigned to the political wilderness.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer poses in his office on Nov. 9 for a group photo with incoming members of his caucus: from left, Ohio's Sherrod Brown, Texas' James Talarico, Iowa's Josh Turek, Michigan's Abdul El-Sayed, North Carolina's Roy Cooper, Illinois' Juliana Stratton, New Hampshire's Chris Pappas, South Carolina's Annie Andrews, Minnesota's Peggy Flanagan, Maine's Troy Jackson and Kansas' Adam Hamilton. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

    It has been revealed that ANALYSIS -- “Life moves pretty fast,” that famed 20th-century philosopher Ferris Bueller once mentioned. “If you don't stop and look around once in a while, you could miss it.”.

    Recent findings suggest that in 2024, Democrats were consigned to the political wilderness. Republicans had captured the White House, flipped the Senate and held the House. President Donald Trump had completely altered the party coalitions as he led the ascendant GOP to victory.

    Industry observers note that now, just two years later, Democrats are on the rise. A historic midterm tsunami has swept them into such commanding Senate and House majorities that some are questioning whether Republicans will ever be in charge again. And if Texas is blue, how does the GOP have any chance in the Electoral College again?

    A major takeaway from the midterm results should be that there’s very little permanence in our politics.

    What may have looked like a fresh GOP coalition was really more of a Trump coalition, and it crumbled in the face of economic frustrations, affordability concerns and the president’s unpopular policies.

    With Trump’s negative job approval rating weighing them down, Republican candidates suffered losses among virtually all demographic groups – including by wide margins among constituencies thought to make up the GOP’s core.

    In a recent development, trump or the Republicans finished ahead among male voters by 4 points in 2018, 8 points in 2020, 14 points in 2022 and 12 points in 2024, according to the exit polls. Men went for Democratic candidates by 4 points (51 percent to 47 percent) this cycle. Meanwhile, Republicans lost even more ground among women. While Kamala Harris finished ahead of Trump by 8 points in 2024, that margin grew to 21 points for Democratic candidates this year.

    Sources indicate that trump closed the gap among Hispanic voters to just 5 points behind Harris two years ago. This year, Hispanic voters nationwide supported Democratic candidates by 32 points (65 percent to 33 percent). Even white voters shifted significantly. They backed Trump or  Republican candidates by 10 points in 2018, 17 points in 2020, 18 points in 2022 and 15 points in 2024. And yet Democrats edged out Republicans by a point (50 percent to 49 percent) on Nov. 3.

    Voters without a college degree were supposed to be a key cog in Republicans’ new populist coalition. But they went from +13 (56 percent to 43 percent) for Trump in 2024 to backing Republican candidates by just 1 point this year. Meanwhile, the gap among voters with a college degree went from 14 points for Harris in 2024 to 30 points for Democrats this cycle.

    In a recent development, republicans had closed the gap among young voters aged 18 to 29 from 35 points in 2018 to just 11 points in 2024. But younger voters supported Democratic candidates this year by 50 points (74 percent to 24 percent). Not to mention Democrats flipped voters aged 45 to 64 for the first time in nearly two decades.

    Industry observers note that white evangelicals appear to be one of the only groups that didn’t shift toward Democrats. They supported GOP candidates 82 percent to 17 percent. But they only made up 17 percent of the electorate, according to the exit polls, which is down from a very consistent 25 percent for more than a decade. So there was still a problem with that group of voters, but it was more about turnout than persuasion.

    While there was an unmistakable leftward shift this year, the results should not be considered a permanent party realignment any more than 2024 was. While Democrats did extremely well in Texas this year, they still haven’t won the Lone Star State in a presidential race in 50 years. So maybe it’s wise for everyone to take a deep breath.

    It has been revealed that if you take this year’s election results and match them with the Senate seats on the ballot in 2028, there doesn’t appear to be a viable path for Republicans back to the majority. But there wasn’t a particularly viable Democratic path to the Senate majority at this point two years ago. And if the Alaska election goes their way, they will end up winning Senate races in seven states that were initially rated Solid Republican.

    If one party starts to get too comfortable, voters have a way of bringing politicians back down to earth. If Democrats come to Congress and push too far to the left or become too defined by their most extreme members, they will squander the opportunity they earned this year.

    The dramatic demographic swings should be evidence that many voters are not beholden to either party and are open to switching allegiances, particularly in a time of economic uncertainty.

    At the same time, if Republicans don’t go through some time of reflection and instead triple down on the policies that led to the blue wave, they risk cementing some of the shifts that started this cycle. It just won’t be thick cement.

  • Trip delay protection reimburses reasonable out-of-pocket expenses such as lodging, meals, toiletries and local transportation when a trip paid for with an eligible card is delayed beyond a set threshold for a covered reason.
  • Coverage typically requires you to pay upfront and then file a claim for reimbursement, and it is secondary to any compensation provided by the airline or other sources.
  • Policies differ in how soon coverage begins, the maximum reimbursement allowed, and whether limits apply per traveler or per trip, which can significantly impact families or groups.
  • Eligibility, covered reasons for delay, and claim limits vary by card, so reviewing your benefits guide and booking rules is essential before relying on this protection.
  • Coverage usually requires a minimum delay of six hours or an overnight stay, and only applies to specific causes like bad weather or equipment failure.
  • Some cards require round-trip travel or payment of the full trip cost with the card, while others allow coverage for taxes and fees on award travel.
  • Claim limits and eligible family members differ; some cards restrict the number of claims per year or define covered travelers more narrowly.

    #19419. Industry News: American Airlines Officially Discontinues Boeing 777-300ER Flagship First Sales
