    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: American Airlines Officially Discontinues Boeing 777-300ER Flagship First Sales

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (675 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • American Airlines stopped selling Flagship First on its Boeing 777-300ER fleet for travel beginning November 19, 2026, ending the last long-haul international first-class product offered by a US airline.
    • Recent findings suggest that flagship Suites will replace both former premium cabins.
    • Recent findings suggest that before the conversion, each aircraft carried eight Flagship First seats, 52 business seats, and 28 premium economy seats.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    American Airlines stopped selling Flagship First on its Boeing 777-300ER fleet for travel beginning November 19, 2026, ending the last long-haul international first-class product offered by a US airline. The cutoff removes eight seats from every aircraft in the 20-jet fleet. American disclosed the date on September 2, the day its first retrofitted 777-300ER entered revenue service between Latest York JFK and Buenos Aires. Business class is now the highest cabin customers can buy on the type.

    Recent findings suggest that flagship Suites will replace both former premium cabins. The retrofitted layout holds 70 lie-flat suites in a 1-2-1 arrangement, along with premium economy recliners and Main Cabin Extra seats, raising total capacity from 304 to 330. The aircraft, first delivered in 2012, was American’s only widebody with separate first and business cabins, and it serves long-haul routes from Miami, Dallas/Fort Worth, Los Angeles, Newly introduced York JFK, and Charlotte to cities including London, Tokyo, São Paulo, and Sydney.

    Recent findings suggest that before the conversion, each aircraft carried eight Flagship First seats, 52 business seats, and 28 premium economy seats. The first class cabin came with private airport check-in and a dedicated fine dining experience at select airports. Under the new structure, all 70 passengers in the forward cabin receive identical service, including priority check-in, security, boarding, and baggage handling. Eight of the suites carry the Flagship Suite Preferred label, with up to 19% more bed space and 42% more living area than the standard suite, and Afar reports that they inherit features once reserved for first class.

    Cabin Configuration of Each 777-300ER.

    Boeing 777-300ER (Legacy Flagship).

    Boeing 777-300ER (Flagship Suites).

    The wider refresh benefits other passengers as well. Every seat now has a personal entertainment screen, a feature the old main cabin lacked, and AAdvantage members receive free WiFi sponsored by AT&T, which was previously sold separately. Bluetooth connectivity, 4K screens, and power are standard throughout. American also expanded Flagship Dining access to all Flagship customers, and lounge access remains available where offered.

    In a recent development, american is the last of the three largest network carriers to drop a separate international first class, following United and Delta, which gave up the cabin years ago. Inc. concluded that all three have judged a standalone first cabin no longer worth the floor space it occupies. Reuters reporting carried by KSL ties the move to carriers chasing higher-spending travelers.

    According to recent reports, the seat math supports that reading. The Points Guy counted 60 lie-flat seats before the retrofit and 70 after, and premium economy grows from 28 to 44 seats. American notes the result is more premium seats than any other US carrier operates on a single aircraft. United, the only other US operator of the 777-300ER, retrofitted its fleet in 2019 to hold up to 60 business class seats, which leaves American with the larger premium cabin on the type.

    According to recent reports, transcontinental Flagship First follows on March 28, 2027, with the cutoff tied to more Airbus A321XLR aircraft entering the fleet. The A321 Transcon subfleet, which serves only Boston, Los Angeles, Latest York, Orange County, and San Francisco, presently offers ten first class and 20 business seats, and American has been converting those jets to a standard domestic first class layout. The A321XLR, by comparison, carries 20 Flagship Suites with 155 total seats.

    On the widebody side, American looks to retrofit all 20 777-300ERs by the end of 2027. The first aircraft, registered N718AN, spent eight months out of service in Hong Kong for its interior work, an indication of the scale of the program. The sources reviewed do not say how aircraft awaiting retrofit will be configured or sold after November 19, so travelers booking in the near term may want to confirm the cabin on their specific flight. Flagship Suites already fly on the 787-9 and the A321XLR, so the 777-300ER conversion carries the brand across three fleets. Chief Commercial Officer Nat Pieper called the aircraft “the next evolution of premium travel at American”.

    End Of An Era: American Retires Boeing 777 Flagship First Class

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (981 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, american Airlines has just officially “retired” its Flagship First product on the Boeing 777-300ER, meaning that no US carrier offers an international first class product anymore.
    • As I’ve covered in the past, American is in the process of eliminating its “premium” first class product, and that change was just implemented for flights as of this week on the carrier’s biggest planes.
    • Recent findings suggest that specifically, the Boeing 777-300ER is American’s “flagship” aircraft, with 20 of the planes in the fleet.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, american Airlines has just officially “retired” its Flagship First product on the Boeing 777-300ER, meaning that no US carrier offers an international first class product anymore. The good news is that an updated business class product is in the process of being rolled out, and that’s something that should benefit a lot of travelers.

    As I’ve covered in the past, American is in the process of eliminating its “premium” first class product, and that change was just implemented for flights as of this week on the carrier’s biggest planes.

    Recent findings suggest that specifically, the Boeing 777-300ER is American’s “flagship” aircraft, with 20 of the planes in the fleet. As of this week, the airline is no longer selling first class on these planes. Now, plenty of 777-300ERs with these cabins are still flying around, as American has just started reconfiguring its 777-300ERs with latest cabins, including the new business class.

    It has been revealed that still, for flights effective immediately, first class seats are just being sold as standard business class seats, and any business class passenger can select seats in the first two rows (you’d think they’d try to charge extra or at least reserve them for select elite members, but nope). So there will no longer be a differentiated soft product… not that there was much of a difference as of late anyway!

    With this change, no US carrier offers an international first class product anymore either, so it very much is the end of an era. American’s 777 first class seats were controversial — on the one hand, I kind of love how they swivel, though on the other hand, they really lack privacy, and the soft product left a lot to be desired.

    In a recent development, I expect we’ll continue to see these planes flying around well into late 2027, or possibly even into 2028, depending on how fast the retrofit project happens. American’s dedicated first class ground product has also largely been discontinued, as Flagship First Dining has turned into Flagship Dining, so a la carte lounge dining is now available to eligible business class passengers as well.

    It’s great that these planes will be getting new business class suites, as they’ll also be the aircraft belonging to a US carrier with the most business class seats, as they’ll have 70 of them… that’s lot!

    While American has now eliminated its international first class product, it’s worth emphasizing that the airline still technically has a “premium” first class, in the sense of a cabin above business class.

    Specifically, American still has its specially configured Airbus A321T aircraft, which are used primarily for flights between New York (JFK) and Los Angeles (LAX) and San Francisco (SFO). The planes have 10 reverse herringbone seats spread across five rows, in a 1-1 configuration.

    American also prepares to eliminate this product, as the A321Ts will be reconfigured into standard A321 domestic configuration aircraft, and A321XLRs will be taking over the transcon routes.

    According to recent reports, american has stopped selling first class on these planes for flights as of March 28, 2027. After that date we’ll still see some of the planes flying with the cabins, but the first class seats will simply be sold as business class.

    American Airlines has officially eliminated its international first class product, as Boeing 777-300ERs no longer have Flagship First for sale. These planes are being retrofitted, as first class seats are being eliminated, and new business class suites are being introduced. However, the planes will keep flying around with the current cabins for quite some time, and business class passengers can freely assign the first class seats.

    In the spring, we’ll see American eliminate its last “premium” first class product, which is the A321T first class cabin, as those planes are replaced by A321XLRs.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    We’ve just seen American formally retire its Boeing 777 first class, and with that, no airline in the United States has a “true” international first class anymore. It’s the end of an era, because going back many decades, premium products were largely pioneered by US carriers. So I think this raises the question — why can US carriers not make first class work in a way that’s economically viable, especially as they keep talking about how premium they are?

    Before we get into this, let me make sure we’re all on the same page when it comes to terms. This post isn’t about the premium cabin on domestic flights, which is often referred to as first class. Instead, it’s about international flights that have a cabin above business class, when it’s marketed as first class. So this would include airlines on my list of the world’s best first class products.

    In a recent development, airline executives are divided on the merits of having an international first class cabin. Some insist that there’s no need for such a cabin, as business class has improved so much. Meanwhile others absolutely see merit to such a product.

    Industry observers note that I mean, just look at how carriers like Air France, Lufthansa, Singapore Airlines, and SWISS, are all investing in first class. I think Air France’s La Premiere first class is the perfect example of the upside such a product has for an airline:.

    It has been revealed that what’s interesting is that for the airlines that succeed with first class, the single biggest market — and single biggest point of sale — is the United States. So how is it that carriers like Air France, Lufthansa, SWISS, etc., can make money offering first class to the United States (primarily targeting Americans), but US airlines seemingly can’t?

    Recent findings suggest that the US has way too many people with tens or hundreds of millions of dollars, or even billions of dollars. There are plenty of people who would pay to fly private, and would pay for Air France La Premiere first class, but would never consider paying the high price for first class on a US carrier, because it’s just not worth it.

    When they fly first class, they want this….

    In a recent development, it’s no surprise that first class at US carriers has historically failed. In many ways, it reflects the failures of the industry from decades past. In other words, first class has long been thought of as “upgrade class,” rather than something actually worth paying for. US carriers have managed to change that narrative on domestic flights, but not so much on international flights.

    According to recent reports, what explains the failure of first class at US carriers? If you ask me, here are the main factors:.

    Recent findings suggest that call it a hot take, but I think international first class absolutely could succeed at a US carrier, if done right, with a couple of caveats.     If those hurdles could be overcome, here’s the play, as I see it (and yes, this is largely inspired by Air France La Premiere):.

    I think the halo effect of something like this would be massive as well. Seriously, US airline executives love to talk about how premium they are, but they can’t even introduce a top-end product, despite having access to the most lucrative customer base in the world.

    In terms of economics, let me also point out that the opportunity cost of a first class cabin isn’t actually that high. “Premium” is all the rage, so what you do here is eliminate some economy seats:.

    At this point, no airline from the United States offers first class on international flights anymore. For airlines that can’t stop talking about how unbelievably premium they are, I find that to be a pretty perplexing reality. I know that many people have just accepted “oh, a good business class is the future,” but I have a different take.

    I think no US carrier actually being able to offer a globally competitive product is a failure in strategy and creativity. They have access to the world’s most lucrative customer base, and other airlines can seemingly make money serving US customers with a first class product. The matter is, US carriers have long not actually given people a reason to fly first class, all while offering too much capacity.

    Personally I think there would be a lot of merit to an international first class product that’s boutique, and is operated in the right markets. That’s not to say that I think it’ll happen — I don’t — but I do think it could succeed. The only real hurdle to overcome would be how to ensure good service….

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, rep.-elect Mark Teixeira reacts after drawing the worst chip during Tuesday’s lottery for newly elected members of Congress.
    • As far as birthdays go, Rep.-elect Shannon Taylor was having a pretty good one.
    • Crowded into a room in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday morning with the rest of her freshman class, the Virginia Democrat walked up to a table with a wooden box and reached in.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, rep.-elect Mark Teixeira reacts after drawing the worst chip during Tuesday’s lottery for newly elected members of Congress. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    As far as birthdays go, Rep.-elect Shannon Taylor was having a pretty good one.

    Crowded into a room in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday morning with the rest of her freshman class, the Virginia Democrat walked up to a table with a wooden box and reached in.

    “This is so nervewracking,” she said, before pulling out a chip with a “1” printed on it.

    It has been revealed that her prize was a coveted one — first choice of office space. Every two years, incoming members of the House play a game of chance to see who can land the best real estate and who will be relegated to less desirable corners of the Capitol complex.

    The room broke out in raucous applause and a standing ovation. Her newly introduced colleagues started singing “Happy Birthday.”.

    Not everyone was so lucky. Rep.-elect Mark Teixeira, R-Texas, pulled number 105 — the very last one. The former MLB player raised his arms in a mock celebration.

    “Lets all hope for the luck of the Taylors,” mentioned Rep.-elect Brent Taylor, R-Tenn., only to emerge with number 81.

    The newly-elected members got their turn in a random order, walking up one by one to a table where deputy executive director of House Office Buildings Kornell Rancy kept watch over the box of chips.

    Rep.-elect John Cowan, R-Ga., was the first to pick a number. The first neurosurgeon to be elected to Congress, Cowan wore his white doctor’s coat as he pulled number 11 out of the box.

    “I wanted to do something where I’m just representing health care providers around the country,” Cowan mentioned.

    In a recent development, as returning members lay claim to more desirable offices made available by those who resign, retire or lose elections, the space they’ve abandoned is left for the newcomers, who are on the Hill this week for orientation. Many of them will end up in the Longworth Building, where suites can be awkward or cramped.

    Industry observers note that not all offices are created equal, and the calculus has changed over the years. The previously undesirable Cannon Building just underwent a budget-busting renovation that lasted more than a decade, with a spacious courtyard opening earlier this year. But the coveted Rayburn Building still retains its prestige, despite repeated and dire warnings from the Architect of the Capitol about its crumbling infrastructure.

    “You’re welcome,” noted Rep.-elect Amish Shah, D-Ariz., after pulling a disappointing number 94.

    Prior to the lottery, Rep.-elect Trever Nehls, R-Texas, was hoping for the best but had a backup blueprint in case his number stated otherwise.

    Sources indicate that “If I don’t pick number one, I’m going to offer one of these cigars as a trade to whoever gets it,” he said, pointing to three of them sticking out of his jacket pocket. He’s preparing to take over the seat currently held by his twin brother Troy, who shares a fondness for stogies.

    The office space lottery dates back to 1908, when members of the 60th Congress received their first office assignments after the completion of what would be named the Cannon Building. A House page drew names and numbers from a box, and members selected their offices from a chart, according to House Office Buildings executive director of facility operations Joe Yates, who kicked things off Tuesday with a history lesson.

    The lottery now is a little more modern, with members poring over virtual office layouts and doing walkthroughs of spaces on laptops.

    According to recent reports, “If somebody had to get 105, I’m glad it was me because I am here to serve, and I’m serving my freshman class by picking the worst office,” Teixeira said. “This is low on my priority list.”.

    Some members revealed their lucky draws themselves, while others let Yates break the news.

    “Come visit me,” noted Rep.-elect Chris Gober, R-Texas, after pulling number 2 from the box.

    After the lottery itself, members huddled with their staff to strategize about the next steps — how to leverage their numbers and select the best suites left on the list, while also exploring layouts, paint colors and carpeting.

    Sources indicate that “First and foremost, a good layout, so we can do good work, and people can be comfortable in doing the work, and then a convenient location. Very utilitarian,” mentioned Rep.-elect Scott Wiener, D-Calif., of his priorities.

    “We’ll get a decent Longworth office,” said Wiener, who drew pick 43. “Cannon would have been ideal, but I’m happy with any office.”.

    Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel, D-Colo., was hoping to replicate the good luck of some of his colleagues. “I’m going to do the Shannon Taylor and Sam Forstag. It’s eyes closed, behind the back,” he stated of his moves, reaching into the box. But it wasn’t enough, and Rutinel pulled number 69.

    “These are not red numbers, these are not blue numbers. These are the remaining numbers, and there ain’t that many,” noted Rep.-elect Johnny Garcia, D-Texas, who was among the last few people to pick. He emerged with number 75.

    And when Rep.-elect Joe Strada, R-Fla., the last of the incoming members to draw, walked up to the table, the whole room cheered.

    “Wouldn’t it be crazy if I picked number 1?” he joked, pulling out the last chip in the box.

    Why I’d Pick Economy Over Premium Economy On An Overnight Flight

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (812 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I just got back to Rio after a quick trip to Ireland for Aer Lingus’ event to showcase their new A330 cabins, including its first-ever premium economy.
    • Recent findings suggest that I flew Air France economy both ways, and I’m glad I resisted the offer of $420 during online check-in to upgrade the outbound overnight economy leg.
    • premium economy question, it all comes down to maximising comfort, and I think this is easier to do in economy than premium economy.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I just got back to Rio after a quick trip to Ireland for Aer Lingus’ event to showcase their new A330 cabins, including its first-ever premium economy.

    Recent findings suggest that I flew Air France economy both ways, and I’m glad I resisted the offer of $420 during online check-in to upgrade the outbound overnight economy leg. Ironically, it was the long day-flight back where I actually wished I’d upgraded.

    However, to answer the economy vs. premium economy question, it all comes down to maximising comfort, and I think this is easier to do in economy than premium economy.

    If, like me, sleeping upright or on your back is almost impossible, then what follows will likely apply to you.

    The main reason I’m deterred to pick premium economy for overnight flights is because of the fixed armrests, where tray tables are sometimes stowed in this cabin.

    Despite the extra recline and leg rest element (which sometimes makes it even harder to get comfortable), the fixed armrests restrict the ability to sleep any way other than straight like a pencil.

    To make matters worse, they stop you from lying across more than one seat if you find yourself in an empty row.

    Sources indicate that it’s for that reason that I much prefer economy. While having a row to yourself isn’t guaranteed, there’s at least a chance of being able to move around the cabin, or stretch out into an empty seat. No matter where you sit or how empty the cabin is, you can’t do that in premium economy.

    Another element of my post-trip planning that I expect many of you to relate to is the fact it takes me so long umming and aahing over the best seat to pick.

    Thanks to my Flying Blue Gold status (SkyTeam Elite Plus), I could pick any seat in the economy cabin of the Boeing 777-200ER for free from 72-hours before departure.

    I narrowed it down to an empty seat in the exit row, and the only row of three with an empty middle seat. I didn’t even consider one of the many empty middle rows of four seats in case they filled up before take off and I ended up in an aisle with no window to rest my head. Using the window or plane’s fuselage to rest my head on is the only saving grace for me when trying to sleep sitting upright.

    As the empty exit seat would have the same restricting fixed partition as premium, I decided against that, too.

    In a recent development, after the “boarding complete” announcement was made, the middle seat in my row remained empty, and there were three seats free in the middle of row 25, a row in front. I explained to the girl in the aisle seat that if one of us moved to the other row, we’d both have three seats to ourselves. She didn’t seem to understand my point, and stated she’d prefer to sit in the aisle than us both have three free seats to ourselves.

    I didn’t want to move to the middle seats either, so I got as comfortable as I could using the middle seat and the pillow I brought from home.

    In the end, I did manage to get some half decent curled up shut eye (the thick pillow protected my back from the hard parts of the seat when propped against the fuselage). However, when I went to the loo, I noticed some people in the rear cabin had got lucky and were fast asleep spread across a whole four seats.

    Maybe I’ll take more of a risk next time….

    In a recent development, I’m not saying economy is always a better choice than premium. For example, I’d always recommend Emirates’ pretty darn impressive premium economy over economy, because it genuinely is several steps up from economy.

    If it was up to me, I’d have had a lie-flat seat for the overnight segment. I didn’t, and I’m pretty certain I got better sleep quality curled up across two seats in economy that I would have almost upright on my back in premium.

    Would you ever choose economy over premium economy?

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that kentucky Rep.
    • Comer, whose role as chairman of the House Oversight Committee gave him a powerful platform to investigate Democrats, including former Presidents Joe Biden and Bill Clinton, has launched a run for governor next year.
    • Recent findings suggest that the Republican, who was just elected to a sixth full term representing Kentucky’s 1st District, is seeking to succeed term-limited Democratic Gov.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that kentucky Rep. James Comer, here talking to reporters on Capitol Hill in June, is running for governor. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Sources indicate that kentucky Rep. James R. Comer, whose role as chairman of the House Oversight Committee gave him a powerful platform to investigate Democrats, including former Presidents Joe Biden and Bill Clinton, has launched a run for governor next year.

    Recent findings suggest that the Republican, who was just elected to a sixth full term representing Kentucky’s 1st District, is seeking to succeed term-limited Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear. Kentucky is one of three states holding off-year gubernatorial elections in 2027, alongside Louisiana and Mississippi.

    In his announcement at a tele-town hall Monday night, Comey emphasized pocketbook problems, pledging to eliminate the state income tax and boost job-creation in Louisville.

    “If we get that income tax to zero, people are going to have more money to spend, and we're going to be able to attract more good-paying jobs to Kentucky, which will be able to keep our best and brightest in the state,’’ he remarked.

    As the leader of the House Oversight panel, Comer has been at the forefront in the fight over the release of records related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. (Last week, the committee released a report concluding that the federal government mishandled criminal probes into Epstein’s activities.).

    Comer is a staunch ally of President Donald Trump, who carried Kentucky by 31 points in 2024, and his hard-nosed style of politics is conveyed in a soft-spoken Southern drawl.

    Sources indicate that known back home as Jamie, Comer has deep roots in rural Monroe County, dating back to the late 1700s. Prior to coming to Congress, he operated a farm before serving 11 years in the Kentucky House. In 2011, he was elected as the commonwealth’s commissioner of agriculture.

    Sources indicate that he made an unsuccessful run for governor in 2015, losing the Republican primary by 83 votes to Matt Bevin, who went on to win the general election. The following year, Comer easily won election to the House from his western Kentucky district, succeeding Republican Ed Whitfield.

    It has been revealed that comer has moved promptly to consolidate GOP support for his gubernatorial bid. He already has the backing of Kentucky Sen. Rand Paul and Sen.-elect Andy Barr. Michael Adams, Kentucky’s term-limited secretary of state who’d been seen a potential contender, gave Comer an early endorsement this summer.

    While Comer enters the race as the Republican front-runner, he won’t have the field to himself. Other declared hopefuls include local prosecutor Rick Hardin and distiller Charles “Bruiser” Martin, who appeared on the Discovery Channel show “Moonshiners: Master Distiller.”.

    While Kentucky has in recent decades grown reliably Republican at the federal level, the GOP has won just two gubernatorial elections there over the past half century. Two high-profile Democrats have already released bids to keep the governor’s mansion in party hands: Lt. Gov. Jacqueline Coleman and former state House Majority Leader and Beshear adviser Rocky Adkins, who ran for governor in 2019.

    In a statement Tuesday, the Democratic Governors Association dismissed Comer as “a job-killing, pro-war politician who looks down on everyday Kentuckians.”.

    A Top Frequent Flyer Complained About American Airlines Selling Their Free Upgrade For $91—Gets Told To Delete Their Post

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3094 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that an American Airlines Executive Platinum status member took to twitter to complain that a flight they were taking the next day still had seats available, and American was offering first class to any passenger in coach for just $91, while ignoring their upgrade benefits.
    • Sources indicate that the AAdvantage program offers upgrades to those with Executive Platinum status starting 100 hours prior to departure (not 72 as this member mentions) but that is out of seats that the airline decides to make available at no charge.
    • But what’s drawing reaction is American’s response, “Please delete this from public view.”.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that an American Airlines Executive Platinum status member took to twitter to complain that a flight they were taking the next day still had seats available, and American was offering first class to any passenger in coach for just $91, while ignoring their upgrade benefits. The AAdvantage program offers upgrades to those with Executive Platinum status starting 100 hours prior to departure (not 72 as this member mentions) but that is out of seats that the airline decides to make available at no charge. Here they’re looking for some amount of money from anyone – $91 from a once a year flyer rather than offering a complimentary upgrade to someone who may be generating $20,000 – $50,000 a year in ticket sales or the equivalent value in partner transactions like cobrand credit card spending. But what’s drawing reaction is American’s response, “Please delete this from public view.” We can understand why this feels frustrating. Your loyalty is genuinely appreciated, and we’re sorry this experience left you feeling overlooked. Please delete this from public view and join us in DM.

    Sources indicate that the AAdvantage program offers upgrades to those with Executive Platinum status starting 100 hours prior to departure (not 72 as this member mentions) but that is out of seats that the airline decides to make available at no charge. Here they’re looking for some amount of money from anyone – $91 from a once a year flyer rather than offering a complimentary upgrade to someone who may be generating $20,000 – $50,000 a year in ticket sales or the equivalent value in partner transactions like cobrand credit card spending.

    But what’s drawing reaction is American’s response, “Please delete this from public view.”.

    Industry observers note that we can understand why this feels frustrating. Your loyalty is genuinely appreciated, and we’re sorry this experience left you feeling overlooked. Please delete this from public view and join us in DM.

    @rawdbee We can understand why this feels frustrating. Your loyalty is genuinely appreciated, and we’re sorry this experience left you feeling overlooked. Please delete this from public view and join us in DM.

    — americanair (@AmericanAir) November 18, 2026.

    The key takeaway here is that upgrades are mostly dead, that this is generally true across major U.S. carriers, but hiding this isn’t the reason American Airlines asks this customer to delete their tweet.

    If this passenger is shocked by $91 upgrade offers, wait till they learn about American Airlines selling upgrades to infrequent customers for $40 (or Delta Delta doing it for $26) rather than honoring the promised complimentary benefit. And wait until they learn that pilots have priority over them too while deadheading.

    Recent findings suggest that of course American Airlines “genuinely appreciate[s]” a customer’s loyalty when they’re being given business by someone based on the promise of an upgrade benefit that they don’t actually need to deliver, selling their excess seats for tens of dollars rather than providing those seats the way they traditionally did as a perk for someone that’s provided tens of thousands of dollars of business. They appreciate the customer sticking around even when they’re no longer delivering the perks.

    Lest you think this is uniquely an American Airlines issue, not only have I seen Delta upsell seats for even less than American (on both domestic and long haul international routes), but United Airlines was equally a pioneer of the technique – they used to pitch infrequent flyers not just on the upgrade itself but that a paid upgrade would leapfrog them over a loyal customer.

    I imagine – though American failed to explain this – the reason they’d suggest removing the tweet is because the image of the passenger’s reservation includes the reservation number. A bad actor who sees it might use it to social engineer access to the booking and make changes. It’s not advisable to publicly post a “PNR” (passenger name record) on the internet even if probably nobody does anything with it. Airlines generally tell customers their status upgrades are no longer available on the cheapest (basic economy) fares. Frontier Airlines is introducing first class, but saying even their top Diamond members will only be eligible for complimentary upgrades if they spend extra by buying a bundle. Elites are asked to purchase a lottery ticket on top of their regular ticket for the change of an upgrade, in a game that’s rigged because the airline determines whether there’s a prize at all (narrator: there usually isn’t). My issue isn’t the airline’s right to make this decision that they value $40 from a one a year flyer over rewarding the loyalty of a $30,000 a year customer, or someone spending $200,000 or more on an airline’s credit card (though this may be unwise). Instead, it’s the disconnect between the airline’s marketing and what they now actually deliver. Airlines promise upgrades as a benefit of customer loyalty. For many decades they delivered this. Now they not only fail to deliver it the way they did in the past, that failure is intentional, traded for minor ducats from low value flyers. Earlier this year, American Airlines CEO Robert Isom spoke to investors and explained the strategy selling buy ups instead of giving out free upgrades in the same merchandising category as “pre-purchase bags, checked baggage.” Twenty years ago 90% of first class seats went to upgrades and awards. Ten years ago it was about half. Now only around 12% of seats are left for Delta SkyMiles elite members. And that means on many routes and flights there are no upgrades at all. The real effect of this is to make top status unappealing. It removes upgrades as the argument for status, and that used to be the main motivator. It’s mid-tier status that’s now the sweet spot: priority check-in (shorter lines with bags) priority boarding (overhead bin space) free checked bags extra legroom coach seat The value in being at the top of the list of flyers that do not clear for an upgrade is minimal. Still, the extra value in top status is not zero. I value being able to add an extra segment to an American Airlines itinerary as a backup when my flights are delayed, without having to make the decision to switch flights right away. For many flyers that’s pretty niche. For most it’s not worth chasing. Delta works to convince flyers that extra legroom economy seats are an upgrade (“The biggest trick the devil in Atlanta ever played was convincing flyers he doesn’t exist”). They even run an upgrade process to get into those seats. But that just reinforces the notion that status which is sufficient to get into these extra legroom seats is all you need to work to attain. The problem for airlines isn’t just that this reduces the incentive for their best customers to keep flying with them. It’s that elite members are the ones most likely to get and spend on their credit cards. And they’ve been leaning into status as the biggest reason for these customers to focus their spending this way. What I’d like to see is airlines return to offering meaningful benefits even in the face of monetizing unsold first class seats for tens of dollars to once a year customers. They could offer a discount on paid upgrades in lieu of complimentary upgrades. American Airlines will already discount their tickets, including award tickets, all day long – employees and family members can book ‘AA20’ fares for 20% off. Other airlines have similar programs. So offering upgrades at 20% off for elites could make real sense. Similarly, cobrand cardmembers at Delta and United get discounts on award redemption (at Delta this is really just charging non-cardmembers more). That model could be replicated with upgrades. They could bring back middle seat blocking on flights that aren’t full, keeping the seats next to top elite members empty until they’re actually needed at the gate. That’s easier to manage now that much of gate work is being automated. I use a $70 per hour rubric on whether it was worth paying to upgrade, though this is dependent on whether I think I’ll get the upgrade free, anyway (and the cheaper the upgrade, the more likely the airline thinks they won’t sell the seat) and what seat I already have (an exit row aisle makes me less likely to pay than a middle seat in back of regular coach). The truth is though that on a flight up to 1,500 miles I’m perfectly happy with an exit row aisle, secured with status. And I’ve been.. fine? First class gets me a bit of extra seat width, but the meal isn’t worth the buy up and I’m generally not day drinking on domestic flights. I plug in and focus on work for the full flight and barely notice my surroundings.     📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, loyalty Lobby flagged Accor’s pre-Black Friday subscription sale. Combined with a weakened Brazilian currency this creates an opportunity.

    According to recent reports, accor is much bigger than its presence in the United States would have you think. The French hotel tech giant finished September with 5,857 hotels and 885,219 rooms. They operate in more than 110 countries, with a huge presence in Europe and extensive coverage in Asia and Australia.

    It has been revealed that their brands include Fairmont, Raffles, Sofitel and MGallery at the luxury end, along with Swissôtel, Pullman and Mövenpick. Then there are Novotel and Mercure, and the budget ibis brands. U.S. options include Fairmont Austin and Raffles Boston.

    I took advantage of the Bilt status match I wrote about this summer, which offered up to Platinum.

    Accor points are worth 2 euro cents apiece toward eligible hotel stays. The familiar redemption is 2,000 points for €40. Using November 18 exchange rates, that’s about $43.87, or 2.19 U.S. cents per point.

    In a recent development, there’s no hotel award chart. An expensive room requires more points. But you can apply points to paid rates without hunting for a limited supply of standard award rooms, and a lower room rate means fewer points needed also.

    Reward points normally expire after 12 months without eligible earning activity. A qualifying points credit extends the whole balance, even if you earn just one point. Partner earning can keep the account alive without another hotel stay. An active ALL Signature subscription also protects Reward points from expiration.

    It has been revealed that here’s the calculation using the published monthly prices multiplied by 12, less 20%, and November 18 exchange rates. Dollar amounts are rounded.

    Your card’s conversion rate will also differ slightly, and be sure to use a card without foreign transaction fees.

    The Explorer blueprint is the better pure points purchase. You’re buying hotel credit for about 29.8% below its redemption value, compared with 23.8% for Absolute. Absolute buys more points and more status credit, but each redeemable point costs more.

    Industry observers note that you can stack this with ALL Accor+ Explorer, a separate paid membership offering 15% off eligible rates at participating hotels worldwide, plus benefits concentrated in Asia Pacific. Accor uses “Explorer” for both a Signature subscription tier and a different membership. Apparently someone thought that was a good idea.

    Recent findings suggest that buying discounted points and then spending them against an eligible discounted room rate is where this gets better. Combining a 15% room discount with points purchased 29.8% below face value produces about 40.3% off the underlying room price, before the separate membership cost and the rewards you’d otherwise earn.

    There are limits to that stack:.

    In a recent development, signature’s monthly Status points are separate from its redeemable Reward points. Absolute supplies 1,000 Status points a month, or 12,000 over a full year, versus the 14,000 needed for Platinum. Those points count in the calendar year they’re credited and reset at year end.

    There’s also an escape valve if your hotel prepares change: Accor points transfer to airlines.

    According to recent reports, many other partners offer a worse ratio. British Airways, for instance, takes 4,000 Accor points for just 2,000 Avios. Use Iberia for Avios rather than accepting half as many through British Airways.

    At the Explorer subscription price above, you’re acquiring points for about 1.54 cents each. That’s also the acquisition cost of a mile through a 1:1 transfer. But once you have the points, moving them to an airline means giving up about 2.19 cents each in hotel credit.

    Delta fans, take note: You can get some serious bonus miles in the coming weeks by booking a cruise.

    It has been revealed that as of this week, Delta Cruises is offering customers 5 Delta miles for every eligible dollar spent on a cruise. That's up sharply from the standard offer of 2 miles per dollar spent. Terms apply.*.

    Indeed, Delta Cruises says this is the richest accelerated mileage offer it has run all year.

    Meanwhile, you can earn even more Delta miles by taking advantage of this promotion and paying for your cruise with a Delta SkyMiles-branded credit card. More on that below.

    It has been revealed that note that you must act fast to get the bonus miles. The accelerated Delta Cruises mileage offer is only available through Dec. 15. It applies to upcoming bookings for cruises scheduled between now and Dec. 31, 2027.

    The Delta Cruises bonus miles offer is available to customers who book any cabin on any of the cruise brands available through Delta Cruises.

    These include all the major cruise brands, such as Royal Caribbean, Carnival Cruise Line, Norwegian Cruise Line, MSC Cruises and Princess Cruises, as well as many smaller ocean, expedition and river cruise lines.

    Sources indicate that among the caveats: Bonus miles are earned per cabin and are awarded to only one passenger per cruise booking. In addition, to qualify, customers must book through the Delta Cruises program at cruises.delta.com.

    Also, the number of miles that customers earn as part of the promotion is based on the total cruise purchase price excluding port charges, port expenses, travel protection, taxes and fees charged at the time of booking.

    There is no limit to the number of miles a customer can earn under the promotion.

    Miles will post to Delta SkyMiles accounts six to eight weeks after the cruise is completed, according to Delta Cruises.

    It has been revealed that you can maximize your purchase by using a Delta SkyMiles credit card, such as the , which earns 1 mile per dollar spent on cruises. With this card, you can find out your offer and see if you are eligible for as high as 80,000 bonus miles after you spend $2,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer. Terms apply.*.

    It has been revealed that bonus Mileage Offer: SkyMiles Members will earn three (3) extra miles per eligible $1 (total of 5 miles per $1) spent on any completed sailing booked through cruises.delta.com. Eligible dollars include the base cruise rate charged at the time of booking, but excludes port charges, port expenses, travel protection, taxes, fees, gratuities, room service, and other incidental charges. Bonus mileage awards are based on upcoming cruise bookings made through Delta Cruises between 11/16/2026, and 12/15/2026, departing from11/17/2026 through 12/31/2027. SkyMiles number must be provided prior to embarkation for bonus mileage offer to be fulfilled. Bonus miles are awarded to only one passenger per cruise booking. Delta reserves the right to change the Delta SkyMiles Program at any time without notice. Delta is not responsible for products or services offered by other participating companies. Please allow 6 - 8 weeks after cruising for miles to be posted to your Delta SkyMiles account. Cruises must be paid for in U.S. currency.     #19395. FAA Ground Stop Blamed On Elon Musk—Here’s Why That’s Ridiculous

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 45m • 📚 Deep Dive (9024 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Viewfromthewing ↗ Open Full Page

    FAA Ground Stop Blamed On Elon Musk—Here’s Why That’s Ridiculous

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 45 min read (9024 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~45 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Friday’s nationwide FAA ground stop followed a contractor’s router installation in Arkansas.
    • There’s a real oversight question here.
    • The November 13 nationwide departure stop began at 3:54 p.m.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Friday’s nationwide FAA ground stop followed a contractor’s router installation in Arkansas. Now the story is becoming about Elon Musk: a claim that DOGE cut FAA employees, oversight was loosened, and this led to the flight stoppage. There’s a real oversight question here. It long predates DOGE. In fact it goes back decades. And even there, the connection between specific oversight failures and what actually happened hasn’t been made. Anyone writing about this needs to at least know that an L3Harris contractor’s router configuration error caused a nationwide air traffic disruption in 2009, too. And federal investigators criticized the FAA’s oversight after that incident! FAA problems did not begin with DOGE. A Router Change Disrupted The National Network The November 13 nationwide departure stop began at 3:54 p.m. Eastern and lasted until 8:15 p.m. Aircraft already airborne continued landing. The FAA’s preliminary account describes excessive connection attempts flooding its telecommunications network. Instability affected 17 of 22 enroute centers and spread to approach facilities. L3Harris had installed a router at a radio site in El Dorado, Arkansas. Investigators also identified a radar site in Amarillo, Texas. Blocking those sites stabilized the network, and officials disabled the relevant function on more than 60 similar routers. FAA Oversight Has Been A Problem, Long Before DOGE One Mile at a Time links the failure to DOGE, drawing on CNN’s reporting about a March 2025 maintenance memo. According to CNN, contractor maintenance shifted from requests requiring approval to notifications that could proceed without explicit approval. Liaisons were still supposed to evaluate the work, but there was a small staff handling thousands of notices. Bedford mentioned the contractor was monitored and a risk assessment occurred. The technicians’ union says the FAA employee merely provided access. An FAA spokesperson later admitted that the escort doesn’t remain during work on L3 equipment. (To be sure, the union saying none of its members performing a risk assessment doesn’t mean nobody performed one.) Additional FAA review might have caught a problem the contractor missed. It’s speculative to suggest that FAA supervision, rathe rthan contractor supervision would have made a difference. And CNN itself describes a chronic technician shortage stretching back years – that I’ve written about several times – as a reason for the policy change. One Mile at a Time though says Elon Musk’s DOGE laid off hundreds of FAA employees, making for the biggest single year layoffs at the organization in history.In fact, the FAA fired 11,400 controllers in 1981. Here there’s no identified fired employee or eliminated review position connected to this installation. Moreover, the Professional Aviation Safety Specialists union announced that its 132 fired probationary employees were being reinstated with back pay, with a March 20, 2025 return date. There were other departures. And it’s plausible DOGE was counterproductive here. I disagreed with the effort overall and didn’t expect success. But there’s just not been anything more than insinuation that that effort was related to Friday’s ground stop. A Harris Router Caused A Nationwide Disruption In 2009 On November 19, 2009, a Harris technician’s router configuration error disrupted the FAA telecommunications network during a transition to fiber. The Transportation Department’s inspector general found that roughly 75% of network routes were blocked. Restoration took five hours. Monitoring failed, and technicians struggled to locate the source. It also found that FAA oversight should have been more effective. Investigators had already called for better equipment configuration controls in 2008. The 2009 outage primarily affected flight planning and data services. But contractor router work, a problem spreading through the network, slow fault detection, and inadequate FAA oversight were documented together in a federal report sixteen years ago with this network and this contractor. The FAA struggled long before the current administration. And maintenance problems go back even further: Government auditors documented a 1997–2000 Alaska experiment that lengthened maintenance intervals and relied heavily on running equipment until failure. A July 2024 aviation industry coalition letter traced a shift toward fixing equipment after it failed to the 2013 budget sequester. As I covered in March, Bob Poole’s reporting describes decades of technician cuts. His sources put the decline at more than 6,600 technicians to roughly 4,000. Insufficient staffing and poor implementation make fixing things after they fail the general path FAA appears to have taken. I Was Skeptical Of DOGE Before Any Of This Happened Musk himself warned about this exact network on February 27, 2025. He claimed an FAA assessment put it “single digit months to catastrophic failure.” He initially blamed Verizon, then corrected himself the same day (the deteriorating system was L3Harris’s). . Elon Musk’s February 27, 2025 correction identifying L3Harris’s legacy network It’s hard to blame Musk when he was literally warning about failure of this specific network. And it highlights the FAA was aware of risk that predated the current administration. Indeed, DOGE was aware of the risk, and its titular head shouted it from the rooftops. I was skeptical that DOGE would fix the FAA when Duffy first invited Musk’s team in. It was asking for a cat, provided it barked. Government agencies behave as they do because of their incentives. Their problems aren’t generally that nobody smart enough or sufficiently determined has shown up to fix them. Cutting employees without changing procurement, funding, and accountability can leave the same dysfunctional institution with less ability to do its work. Singapore is an unusual example of building substantial state capacity, something of an outlier. Lee Kuan Yew deliberately recruited top talent into a prestigious public service, promoted on merit, strengthened corruption enforcement, and later added high pay. Its competence was built through institutions, rewards, and consequences. We get the government that we have for public choice reasons, and because of median voters. Three are companies that benefit from the way the system works, employees themselves, and both groups have much greater incentive to pay attention to the details than the average citizen. The programs we have, that many even deem wasteful, exist for a reason – not because of systemic incompetence. Someone benefits! The FAA Has Spent Decades Failing To Deliver Promised Upgrades The FAA was testing replacements for paper flight strips in 1983. It’s still rolling them out. Canada completed its commercial airport and terminal facility rollout by 2006, according to the Eno Transportation Center’s history of the two countries’ efforts. The inspector general’s review of NextGen shows more than $15 billion spent through 2024 and relatively little to show for it. And this administration is repeating familiar mistakes. In September, the Government Accountability Office found 11,389 separate project schedules for the latest modernization efforts, including installations at the same sites without coordinating them to minimize operational disruption. The FAA operates air traffic control and regulates its safety. Different offices handle those jobs, but they remain inside the same agency. The International Civil Aviation Organization guidance calls for independent oversight and separation of responsibilities. The FAA’s 2023 independent safety review found lack of that separation, noting that the oversight office needed the operating organization’s concurrence to gather information. The regulated operation could impede the regulator inside the same agency. I’ve laid out the Canadian alternative. NAV CANADA is a separate nonprofit with stakeholder governance and no equity shareholders. It charges consumers and finances investment with debt instead of waiting for Congress to fund each year’s portion of a long term project. Transport Canada regulates it. The Response To Failure Is Another Request For Billions One Mile at a Time is right to say “There obviously won’t be any accountability with this situation.” But this has been a problem across administrations. An organization that repeatedly misses its technology goals gets to use the resulting obsolescence as an argument for even more money. As I wrote this week, most of the $30.1 billion Modern Skies Act doesn’t even go to air traffic control (a majority goes to airports, primarily St. Louis – in the home state of the bill’s Senate sponsor). Now the administration wants $50 billion. Proposal Air Traffic Systems And Facilities Airport Projects $30.1 billion Modern Skies Act $12.1 billion $18 billion $50.1 billion administration request $30.1 billion $20 billion The upcoming $50.1 billion request includes new control centers and towers as well as technology, but still bundles $20 billion in airport infrastructure and terminal spending into the response to a communications failure. Congress already supplied $12.5 billion last year. More investment may be needed. Users, not taxpayers, should be funding this. And real reforms are needed before handing the FAA tens of billions after their failed management processes squander the last tens of billions. The inspector general’s review of NextGen shows more than $15 billion spent through 2024 and relatively little to show for it. And this administration is repeating familiar mistakes. In September, the Government Accountability Office found 11,389 separate project schedules for the latest modernization efforts, including installations at the same sites without coordinating them to minimize operational disruption. The FAA operates air traffic control and regulates its safety. Different offices handle those jobs, but they remain inside the same agency. The International Civil Aviation Organization guidance calls for independent oversight and separation of responsibilities. The FAA’s 2023 independent safety review found lack of that separation, noting that the oversight office needed the operating organization’s concurrence to gather information. The regulated operation could impede the regulator inside the same agency. I’ve laid out the Canadian alternative. NAV CANADA is a separate nonprofit with stakeholder governance and no equity shareholders. It charges consumers and finances investment with debt instead of waiting for Congress to fund each year’s portion of a long term project. Transport Canada regulates it. The Response To Failure Is Another Request For Billions One Mile at a Time is right to say “There obviously won’t be any accountability with this situation.” But this has been a problem across administrations. An organization that repeatedly misses its technology goals gets to use the resulting obsolescence as an argument for even more money. As I wrote this week, most of the $30.1 billion Modern Skies Act doesn’t even go to air traffic control (a majority goes to airports, primarily St. Louis – in the home state of the bill’s Senate sponsor). Now the administration wants $50 billion. Congress already supplied $12.5 billion last year. More investment may be needed. Users, not taxpayers, should be funding this. And real reforms are needed before handing the FAA tens of billions after their failed management processes squander the last tens of billions.     One Mile at a Time links the failure to DOGE, drawing on CNN’s reporting about a March 2025 maintenance memo. According to CNN, contractor maintenance shifted from requests requiring approval to notifications that could proceed without explicit approval. Liaisons were still supposed to evaluate the work, but there was a small staff handling thousands of notices. Bedford mentioned the contractor was monitored and a risk assessment occurred. The technicians’ union says the FAA employee merely provided access. An FAA spokesperson later admitted that the escort doesn’t remain during work on L3 equipment. (To be sure, the union saying none of its members performing a risk assessment doesn’t mean nobody performed one.) Additional FAA review might have caught a problem the contractor missed. It’s speculative to suggest that FAA supervision, rathe rthan contractor supervision would have made a difference. And CNN itself describes a chronic technician shortage stretching back years – that I’ve written about several times – as a reason for the policy change. One Mile at a Time though says Elon Musk’s DOGE laid off hundreds of FAA employees, making for the biggest single year layoffs at the organization in history.In fact, the FAA fired 11,400 controllers in 1981. Here there’s no identified fired employee or eliminated review position connected to this installation. Moreover, the Professional Aviation Safety Specialists union confirmed that its 132 fired probationary employees were being reinstated with back pay, with a March 20, 2025 return date. There were other departures. And it’s plausible DOGE was counterproductive here. I disagreed with the effort overall and didn’t expect success. But there’s just not been anything more than insinuation that that effort was related to Friday’s ground stop. A Harris Router Caused A Nationwide Disruption In 2009 On November 19, 2009, a Harris technician’s router configuration error disrupted the FAA telecommunications network during a transition to fiber. The Transportation Department’s inspector general found that roughly 75% of network routes were blocked. Restoration took five hours. Monitoring failed, and technicians struggled to locate the source. It also found that FAA oversight should have been more effective. Investigators had already called for better equipment configuration controls in 2008. The 2009 outage primarily affected flight planning and data services. But contractor router work, a problem spreading through the network, slow fault detection, and inadequate FAA oversight were documented together in a federal report sixteen years ago with this network and this contractor. The FAA struggled long before the current administration. And maintenance problems go back even further: Government auditors documented a 1997–2000 Alaska experiment that lengthened maintenance intervals and relied heavily on running equipment until failure. A July 2024 aviation industry coalition letter traced a shift toward fixing equipment after it failed to the 2013 budget sequester. As I covered in March, Bob Poole’s reporting describes decades of technician cuts. His sources put the decline at more than 6,600 technicians to roughly 4,000. Insufficient staffing and poor implementation make fixing things after they fail the general path FAA appears to have taken. I Was Skeptical Of DOGE Before Any Of This Happened Musk himself warned about this exact network on February 27, 2025. He claimed an FAA assessment put it “single digit months to catastrophic failure.” He initially blamed Verizon, then corrected himself the same day (the deteriorating system was L3Harris’s). . Elon Musk’s February 27, 2025 correction identifying L3Harris’s legacy network It’s hard to blame Musk when he was literally warning about failure of this specific network. And it reveals the FAA was aware of risk that predated the current administration. Indeed, DOGE was aware of the risk, and its titular head shouted it from the rooftops. I was skeptical that DOGE would fix the FAA when Duffy first invited Musk’s team in. It was asking for a cat, provided it barked. Government agencies behave as they do because of their incentives. Their problems aren’t generally that nobody smart enough or sufficiently determined has shown up to fix them. Cutting employees without changing procurement, funding, and accountability can leave the same dysfunctional institution with less ability to do its work. Singapore is an unusual example of building substantial state capacity, something of an outlier. Lee Kuan Yew deliberately recruited top talent into a prestigious public service, promoted on merit, strengthened corruption enforcement, and later added high pay. Its competence was built through institutions, rewards, and consequences. We get the government that we have for public choice reasons, and because of median voters. Three are companies that benefit from the way the system works, employees themselves, and both groups have much greater incentive to pay attention to the details than the average citizen. The programs we have, that many even deem wasteful, exist for a reason – not because of systemic incompetence. Someone benefits!     #19394. What Republicans don’t know about Black voters’ resilience cost them

    What Republicans don’t know about Black voters’ resilience cost them

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1019 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, sen.-elect Scott Colom speaks during a victory rally at Tougaloo College on Nov.
    • Recent findings suggest that the campaign of Mississippi’s Sen.-elect Scott Colom was rightfully praised for its clever and brutal ads.
    • Industry observers note that however, it was fitting that the Democrat’s closing message traded the edge for a solemn reminder of who and what brought him so far on his journey to his election as Mississippi’s first Black U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, sen.-elect Scott Colom speaks during a victory rally at Tougaloo College on Nov. 11. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images).

    Recent findings suggest that the campaign of Mississippi’s Sen.-elect Scott Colom was rightfully praised for its clever and brutal ads. The “pick another protein” spot will forever be stuck in the brains of a huge swath of Americans, especially Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith. She underestimated Colom and his team, and will soon be an ex-senator.

    Industry observers note that however, it was fitting that the Democrat’s closing message traded the edge for a solemn reminder of who and what brought him so far on his journey to his election as Mississippi’s first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction.

    The ad delivered an all-American lesson about history, born of bravery and sacrifice.

    Filmed at the Jackson, Miss., home of slain civil rights leader Medgar Evers, the ad featured Colom recounting the story of Evers, a World War II veteran who survived Normandy, only to be shot in the back by a racist assassin, resentful that a Black man dared to exercise his rights as a citizen in the country he fought for.

    In a recent development, “He was killed for helping Mississippians vote,” Colom said. “On Tuesday, use your vote and honor everyone who died for that right.”.

    In a state where voting is still racially polarized, it was clear that Colom would not win over a majority of white voters; he won an estimated 25 percent, better than Democrats in recent elections and cutting into Trump’s margins, but certainly not a path to victory.

    Black voters in Mississippi made the difference, as they often have. With their allies in the cause of justice, they heeded the call. They showed up despite the state’s stringent and often confusing voting restrictions, purges of the voting rolls engineered by Republican Secretary of State Michael Watson (who used unverified data from a credit bureau), and the U.S. Supreme Court Louisiana v. Callais decision that led to a wave of Southern states breaking up Black-majority districts.

    When the Mississippi purges resulted in “affidavit ballots” that required verification to count, as The Washington Post reported, young Black women tracked down those voters, one by one, to do everything they could to ensure voters’ efforts were not in vain.

    Black voters mattered in states all over the country, but especially in the South, where low turnout has plagued Democrats, particularly in midterm elections.

    In a recent development, keisha Lance Bottoms was elected the first Black female governor in the country in Georgia, where Democrats won up and down the ballot. Newly elected senators Annie Andrews in South Carolina and James Talarico of Texas campaigned for and earned support from Black voters with proposals that rose above platitudes. And don’t sleep on North Carolina, where voters flipped seats the GOP tried to gerrymander into a hardened majority. The sight of hundreds of students from HBCU NC A&T State University, denied a campus early voting site, marching to the polls, must have made the ancestors smile.

    In Florida and Louisiana, where Democrats had little financial support and lost their statewide races, Black voters brought them tantalizingly close to victory and energized for the contests to come.

    I still don’t expect Republicans to give up the election shenanigans, done in the name of “election integrity” and color blindness but in reality designed to demoralize as much as suppress. Why try to win over a diverse electorate with an inclusive, policy-driven message when manipulating Black-majority districts can still work?

    The number of Black U.S. House members in the next session of Congress will fall, offset by a few Democrats who survived in redrawn districts, including Shomari Figures of Alabama and Don Davis of North Carolina.

    But you can’t redistrict a state, and you can’t skip town halls and expect tradition, support for the Confederacy and an “R” after your name to forever save you — the Hyde-Smith playbook.

    Industry observers note that "I blocked Scott Colom from being a federal judge, and you blocked him from being U.S. senator," she bragged, too soon, on election night.

    Maybe she should have emphasized affordability, saving rural hospitals and serving all Mississippians, as Colom did.

    What did GOP officials in those Southern red states think they would accomplish by focusing on their base and ignoring everyone else in states they were supposed to be serving?

    Did they not pay attention in history class, or maybe they attended one of those post-integration private schools where an unedited version of America’s past might not have been on the lesson proposal?

    Did they believe that voters who remembered Evers, Fannie Lou Hamer, Vernon Dahmer and countless others would shrug and say “you win” when legislatures and elections officials quickly and cynically pounced to quiet their voices?

    That would be disrespectful to all the people who worked for, sometimes died for rights they knew they may never enjoy, yet had a belief in America and the rightness of their cause.

    According to recent reports, scott Colom and the Evers family remembered. He was emotional in his reaction, in an MS NOW interview, when asked about the statement from Reena Evers-Everette, daughter of Medgar and Myrlie Evers. “Their courage helped make this moment possible,” she remarked.

    Industry observers note that colum agreed: “I absolutely stand on their shoulders. And from the bottom of my heart, I’m going to do everything I can to make them proud.”.

    Post-election, he has been very gracious, saying that he intends to serve all Mississippians, including the woman whom I suspect would hit a different note if the election had turned in her favor.

    I have no doubt Scott Colom means it. He knows who paid the price to get him this far.

She is host of the CQ Roll Call “Equal Time with Mary C. Curtis” podcast. Follow her on X @mcurtisnc3.

    #19392. Some records in Ilhan Omar case will be released, judge says

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (470 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Some records in Ilhan Omar case will be released, judge says

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (470 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., speaks during a news conference at the Capitol last summer.
    • Sources indicate that A judge noted he will order the release of some information about the federal investigation into Rep.
    • Sources indicate that judge James Boasberg for the U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., speaks during a news conference at the Capitol last summer. Few details have emerged so far about the government’s search of her home earlier this fall. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    Sources indicate that A judge noted he will order the release of some information about the federal investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., which included a search of her Washington house last month.

    Sources indicate that judge James Boasberg for the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia made the statement Tuesday during a hearing brought by news organizations and an advocacy group seeking details about the search. Boasberg ordered the government to provide him by Friday what could be disclosed in the case. He pointed to how investigators are handling the “speech or debate” clause immunity that Omar has as a sitting member of Congress.

    “This is purely legal questions, interesting questions, about the privilege, the extent of the privilege and how it would apply,” Boasberg said.

    The Constitution includes an immunity for members of Congress for the “speech or debate” they engage in as part of their jobs.

    Recent findings suggest that boasberg also directed the government to propose redactions to the as-yet secret docket. While he said next week’s expected disclosures would not include the 67-page document that investigators provided to justify the search, he left the door open to unsealing that down the road if the government closes the case or brings charges.

    Justice Department attorney Alessandra Serano argued against broad disclosures, calling it “very rare that a precharging, pre-indictment unsealing would happen.”.

    The high-profile nature of the investigation leaked into the courtroom Tuesday, as Boasberg cited statements by President Donald Trump and others about the investigation into Omar.

    “You have had administration officials, prominent ones, talking about the purpose of the investigation,” Boasberg said.

    Administration officials have accused Omar of committing immigration crimes for years, and Trump said last month the DOJ was looking into Omar “strongly.” Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on a recent podcast that investigators had served multiple search warrants and were investigating possible immigration fraud tied to when Omar entered the United States as a child.

    Separately, Boasberg said he may problem rulings in the coming weeks unsealing portions of other court cases tied to the investigation, including one brought by Omar herself earlier this month seeking the return of the items seized in the search.

    The administration executed the search warrant in October, just a few weeks before the midterm elections. The timing of the search drew accusations of political bias from Democrats who claimed that the administration brought the case to sway the midterm elections.

    For years Trump has noted he wanted criminal charges to be brought against his political foes, including Omar and others in Congress.
